articles.title_orig: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.title_zh: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
articles.content_orig:
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case.
Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague.
Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case.
The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked whether it’s possible the infection was from a bioweapon, “We do not think so.”
“They are saying it is very much under control,” he said, adding “Russia is not saying much either.”
Trump confirmed he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and when asked about what US intelligence agencies are reporting, Trump said the two sides are “in very deep discussions” and that they would likely be able to provide an update “probably tomorrow.”
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute.
“We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.”
“We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said.
WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case.
In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
“We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area.
The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added.
About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.
“What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC.
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

MUMBAI, India, Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DP World has reaffirmed its long-term commitment to India's economic growth and global trade ambitions, as H.E. Essa Kazim, Executive Chairman, made his first visit to the country in his new role, accompanied by Mr. Yuvraj Narayan, Group Chief Executive Officer, and members of DP World's Global Board of Directors.
The visit reflects the strategic importance of India to DP World's global growth agenda and its commitment to building world-class trade and logistics infrastructure in partnership with the country. As India strengthens its position as a global manufacturing, consumption and export hub, DP World continues to invest in capabilities that connect businesses to international markets, enhance supply chain resilience and support the country's evolving trade requirements.
A key engagement during the visit was a meeting with Mr. Gaurav Dayal, IAS, Chairman of the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA) and Mr. Ravish Kumar, IRTS, Deputy Chairman, reaffirming a partnership spanning nearly three decades. Beginning with the concession agreement for Nhava Sheva International Container Terminal (NSICT), the association has played a role in the development of India's public-private partnership model in port infrastructure.
The discussions focused on strengthening this longstanding relationship and exploring opportunities for future collaboration, including the development of Vadhavan Port and further investment in the JNPA Special Economic Zone. The engagement underscored the importance of sustained collaboration between the public and private sectors in developing the infrastructure, connectivity and capacity needed to support India's next phase of trade-led growth.
As part of the visit, H.E. Essa Kazim and Mr. Yuvraj Narayan inaugurated Phase 2 of the Nhava Sheva Business Park (NSBP) in the presence of members of DP World's Global Board of Directors. The business park's first phase spans 44 acres and provides one million square feet of warehousing space. The newly inaugurated second phase covers an additional 42 acres and will add a further one million square feet of warehousing capacity, representing an investment of approximately ₹500 crore ($52 million).
Together, the two phases strengthen DP World's ability to support the growing and increasingly sophisticated requirements of customers across industries.
Commenting on the visit and the company's commitment to India, H.E. Essa Kazim, Executive Chairman, DP World, said, "India is a strategic partner in DP World's global growth journey, and we see significant opportunities to contribute to the country's ambitions as a leading global trading nation. Our commitment goes beyond investing in infrastructure; it is about building enduring partnerships, strengthening connectivity and creating integrated supply chain solutions that enable Indian businesses to compete more effectively in global markets. The expansion of Nhava Sheva Business Park reflects our confidence in India's long-term potential and our continued focus on meeting the evolving needs of our customers. We look forward to deepening our collaboration with government and industry partners to support India's growth and unlock new opportunities for trade."
The expansion is part of DP World's broader vision to develop an integrated logistics ecosystem at Nhava Sheva, connecting port operations with container freight stations, rail, warehousing and Free Trade Warehousing Zone capabilities. By bringing these complementary services together, DP World enables customers to move cargo more efficiently, optimise logistics costs and access end-to-end supply chain solutions through a connected infrastructure network.
The investment reflects a customer-led approach to growth, anticipating changing business needs while providing the capacity, flexibility and connectivity required to serve both domestic and international trade. It also reinforces DP World's focus on developing infrastructure that creates long-term value for customers and contributes to the wider competitiveness of India's logistics sector.

articles.title_orig: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
articles.title_zh: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump's administration has been sued by the Democratic National Committee over government-funded television ads that cast the president in a flattering light. The DNC filed the complaint on Wednesday, arguing the spots break federal spending and propaganda laws.
The party pointed to a measure Trump signed into law this year. It says money appropriated by Congress can't be used "for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress." The suit also invoked the Anti-Deficiency Act. It bars spending money Congress hasn't appropriated, and the Purpose Statute, which limits taxpayer funds to uses Congress has approved .
The DNC calls the spots "campaign-style advertisements." It says they deprive Democrats "of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates." That, the party argues, leaves Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage.
Additionally, watchdog group Common Cause has filed its own suit, making similar arguments that the administration violated appropriations statutes. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget are named as defendants alongside Trump and the White House.
For those unaware, the ads launched last month. They got criticised by lawmakers in both parties, many of whom questioned their legality. On Monday, Trump announced on Truth Social that he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads going forward. He did not say whether the government would be reimbursed for spots already aired. By Tuesday, White House officials told Politico the pledge applied only to future ads.
Some ads have kept running with a disclaimer saying the U.S. government paid for them. The White House wouldn't tell NBC News whether those were bought before or after Trump's pledge. A person familiar with the buy said it ends this week, after which outside groups will cover the cost.

articles.title_orig: Ten years later, Penn’s Perry World House continues to shape global policy
articles.title_zh: Ten years later, Penn’s Perry World House continues to shape global policy
articles.content_orig:
Ten years after Perry World House opened its doors at Penn, the center has adapted to a changing world while retaining its founding mission.
PWH opened in September 2016 following a $10 million gift three years earlier from 1977 Wharton graduate and then-Trustee Richard Perry and his wife, Lisa. Since then, the center has expanded its reach across campus while engaging students, scholars, and policymakers.
In an interview, Political Science professor and PWH Faculty Director Michael Horowitz — who has long been affiliated with the center — said that former Penn President Amy Gutmann envisioned PWH as a way to bring together expertise on global policy issues across Penn’s 12 schools.
The goal, he said, was to “make the whole bigger than the sum of the parts in a way that could create transformational experiences” for the Penn community. In preparation for that role, PWH began its programming even before its physical space opened.
The building replaced the Kappa Alpha Society’s old house on Locust Walk. Most of the old building was torn down, leaving “a huge hole in the ground” during construction , Horowitz explained.

“While all of that construction was going on from 2014 to 2016, World House was starting to ramp up programming across the University,” he added.
Just a year after its opening, the center received nearly $500,000 from the Carnegie Corporation of New York — now known as the Andrew Carnegie Foundation — to assist its Global Innovation Program. The grant-funded workshops and initiatives focused on interdisciplinary conversation and international policy issues.
Over the following years, the center broadened both its programming and its network.
Perry World House panel celebrates Benjamin Franklin’s role at Constitutional Convention
Perry World House announces inaugural cohort of faculty research fellows
“The mission of World House has always been the same,” Horowitz said, describing its focus as “bridging the gap between academia and the policy world.”
One example is its Distinguished Visiting Fellows Program, a key avenue for connecting Penn students and faculty with policymakers, government officials, and scholars from around the world. The program, which has existed since PWH’s inception, has a cohort of 14 global leaders this academic year.
While its institutional values have remained steady, other aspects of PWH have changed over time.
When it first opened, the center’s work focused on two broad themes: global order and global shifts. In summer 2024, the center reorganized its work around security, climate change, global justice and human rights, and democracy.
“World House is an institution that is supposed to reflect a changing world, and so what we do reflects that as well,” Horowitz said.
Political Science professor Beth Simmons, a member of PWH’s faculty council, said the change was intended to give the center “a little more precision” in what it focused on. She explained that the revised structure better matched the faculty, visiting fellows, and other resources the center has built over time.
“When it was first established, it had no built-in networks or anything like that — those had to be developed over time,” Simmons said. “It took true dedication by the staff, by the University to fund the efforts, by the faculty, by various people who have come in contact with the Perry World House.”
Faculty involvement has expanded alongside the center’s growth. According to Horowitz, PWH engaged more than 200 faculty members from all 12 of Penn’s schools during the last academic year.
The center also recently launched a Faculty Fellows program built around its four research areas.
“These faculty fellow projects are a way for World House to not just build broad relationships with lots of faculty, but deep relationships with faculty who are already doing transformational research,” Horowitz said. “What World House can help them do is connect with the global policy world to have impact.”
Student engagement is also a central part of PWH’s work, with three distinct programs offered. One of them, the World House Student Fellows program, includes 31 students from all four of Penn’s undergraduate schools this year.
Students participate in weekly seminars, work on yearlong policy projects, and travel to meet policymakers and other global affairs professionals.
College senior Ashti Tiwari, a World House Student Fellow and former staffer for The Daily Pennsylvanian, said that the program has shaped much of her experience at Penn.
“Places like Perry World House help you make sense of the world and the global issues of the world,” she said.
She also pointed to the interdisciplinary nature of the center.
“They really do try to bring people together from all parts of campus,” Tiwari said.
Evan Stubbs, a College senior who was previously a World House Student Fellow and a DP staffer, said the program gave him opportunities to engage directly with international policy organizations.
“I don’t know if those opportunities would really exist without Perry World House facilitating the connections and guiding people’s interests,” Stubbs said.
Through PWH, he had the opportunity to travel to Washington, New York, and Geneva. He also worked on a policy project with the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research.
Stubbs also said that the program serves a “dual purpose” by helping students pursue policy opportunities they are passionate about while also giving organizations a way to recruit Penn students.
As PWH enters its second decade, Horowitz said that further increasing student involvement will be a priority.
“Our task over the next decade is to continue to integrate Penn students even more into our thinking and programming and activities in a way that helps create transformational opportunities to help shape not just people’s careers, but how they think,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike’s Lawyers Say She Is Angry and Confused After Failed Execution
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike’s Lawyers Say She Is Angry and Confused After Failed Execution
articles.content_orig:
A judge sided with the Tennessee inmate and ruled that evidence from her botched execution should be preserved.
• Christa Pike’s attorneys said they believed she was “brain-dead” after her botched execution last week – before she woke up and started talking. She is “ angry and confused about everything right now,” but is “very aware that the state tried to execute her,” attorney Randy Spivey told reporters. Pike has a “long road to recovery,” he added.
• The attorneys spoke after they were granted an emergency motion ordering the state to preserve evidence related to the execution. This includes 911 calls and communications between any state officials as well as physical evidence, Judge I’Ashea Myles said.
• Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Our live coverage has ended. Scroll down for updates on today’s court hearing and the latest from Christa Pike’s attorneys following her botched execution.
A judge ruled today the state of Tennessee must preserve all evidence related to Christa Pike’s failed execution.
This includes 911 calls and communications between any state officials as well as physical evidence, Judge I’Ashea Myles said, after hearing arguments.
Pike is conscious and speaking, her attorneys said, despite it appearing the night before that she was brain-dead and would be taken off life support. She was hospitalized after surviving two ostensibly lethal doses of pentobarbital last week.
Lauren del Valle, Maureen Chowdhury, August Phillips and Rebekah Riess contributed reporting.
Lawyers for a Texas man are asking a judge to pause his execution , citing the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week.
Jamaal Howard is set to be executed by lethal injection later today , the first since Pike. Howard, 46, was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery.
In the filing, the attorneys requested more information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use, the AP reported.
Pike’s lawyers allege that issues with IV lines allowed the barbiturate to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream .
There is another execution scheduled in Florida next week, a state that has carried out the most executions so far this year, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . All of them used lethal injection, data shows.
Michelle Nowell, a Tennessee resident, said the state has “paid enough” for Christa Pike, citing the state’s rising bill from the continuation of her case after her botched execution last week.
“We have paid for Christa Pike, and now we’re paying for attorneys, and now we’re paying for hospital bills, and now they’re talking about lawsuits,” Nowell told CNN. “And the worst part is that Colleen has been forgotten.”
Pike was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at a job training facility.
Nowell pushed back on Pike’s attorneys statement describing her botched execution as “cruel and unusual” and to those who say Pike has “changed” in her more than 30 years in prison.
“Colleen is the one that knew cruel and unusual punishment,” she said.
Nowell said the state handled Pike’s execution “absolutely terribly.”
“I think it’s shameful,” Nowell said. “I’m a Tennessean, born and raised, a voter, and I know that our governor is going to be leaving soon, in January, and my hope is that Gov. (Bill) Lee will do the right thing and follow through with this execution.”
Jerri Green, Tennessee’s Democratic candidate for governor, who is running against Republican US Sen. Marsha Blackburn, has vowed to “enact a moratorium on all future executions,” in the state.
“True respect for the victims and their families means a justice system built on honesty, fairness, and safety, not cruelty, endless systemic failure, and secrecy. The facts are clear: the death penalty has proven to be an ineffective deterrent to violent crime, it is vastly more expensive than life imprisonment, and it is riddled with bias,” her statement reads in part.
“While the rest of the world reels from a botched execution that went horribly wrong, Blackburn is doubling down, calling to bring back the electric chair. That is barbaric, and it has no place in our state,” Green said of her opponent.
“As a public defender who has seen the devastating flaws in our justice system firsthand, my stance remains unshakeable: true pro-life values mean rejecting the death penalty entirely, and as Governor, I will enact a moratorium on all future executions,” she added.
Christa Pike’s attorney requested that her hand be unshackled as she receives medical care at a hospital after her botched execution.
Myles asked Ihnen had an affidavit from the medical personnel stating this request, and the attorney said he didn’t, but could provide it. The judge said she would make a decision after the document is submitted.
The state interjected on the request and pointed to Pike’s “escape history.” The judge said the request only includes unshackling Pike’s hand, not feet, and that she is reserving her judgment on this matter until she hears from the medical personnel.
Christa Pike’s attorney said he noticed “extraordinary” swelling of her hands following her botched execution attempt.
“Her hands looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” he said. “The swelling was extraordinary, and that’s, that’s probably as far as I can go.”
Earlier, in court, her attorneys requested that Pike’s hand be unshackled while she is in the hospital due to the “extensive damage done to her arms and hands.”
Attorneys for Christa Pike thought she was brain-dead Monday and would be taken off life support the following day, but “to the shock of everyone,” on Tuesday, she woke up and began to talk, attorney Randy Spivey with the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender said.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery,” Spivey said.
Pike has pneumonia and a blood clot in one of her arms, and she is not able to swallow yet and is therefore not eating, according to Spivey.
“She cannot move either of her arms. Both of her arms and hands are tremendously swollen, and we do not know what, if any, function she will regain in her arms. But we do know that there’s a long road ahead,” he added.
The botched execution of Christa Pike was “foreseeable and foreseen,” one of her lawyers, Randy Spivey, reiterated today after a court hearing to preserve evidence after the incident.
“What happened to Christa is exactly what the state was warned would happen, and there are so many questions that need to be answered, not by Christa — but by the state of Tennessee,” he said at a news conference outside the courthouse.
Her lawyer said Pike was “at peace” in the moments before her execution. She was “kind and polite” as officials struggled to set the IV lines for more than an hour, Spivey said.
“And then she woke up in a hospital surrounded by people she didn’t know with a tube down her throat. We don’t know the toll all of this will take, but Christa is a survivor, and we remain hopeful,” Spivey said.
Pike’s attorneys previously said they had warned courts beforehand that Pike’s vein issues would make it difficult to carry out the lethal injection.
An attorney for Christa Pike said today he understood that the first thing she said upon waking up yesterday was, “Where am I and who are you?”
The attorney, Randy Spivey from the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender, noted at a news conference after today’s hearing that he was not personally in the room when she woke up and did not want to speculate.

articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
articles.content_orig:
Update: Isaias became a hurricane late Wednesday night. See the latest forecast here .
Tropical Storm Isaias was "quickly intensifying" and is expected to approach the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center .
Currently swirling in the Gulf, Isaias would be the Atlantic basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. An El Niño climate pattern continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season , which ends Nov. 30.
Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday and make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast of the U.S. late Friday or early Saturday, the hurricane center said.
A hurricane warning was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Florida's Bay/Gulf county line, and a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to Ocean Springs, and from the Bay/Gulf county line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was also issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida, according to the hurricane center.
Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 60 miles from the storm's center on Wednesday evening. Its maximum sustained winds were 70 mph, and it was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday morning, the hurricane center said.
A storm's maximum wind speed must rise to at least 74 mph to be considered a hurricane.
Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see rainfall ranging from 1 to 5 inches, forecasters said.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.
The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."
At high tide, the approximately 300-mile stretch between Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and Indian Pass, Florida, could see a storm surge of up to 7 feet, forecasters said, potentially causing major flooding.
In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."
On Wednesday, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a similar state of emergency for 40 counties, saying in a statement that it will allow Alabama officials "to take any needed steps ahead of landfall."
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017) and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

articles.title_orig: Japan ranked best country in the world for fourth straight year
articles.title_zh: Japan ranked best country in the world for fourth straight year
articles.content_orig:
Japan was named the world’s most attractive country for the fourth consecutive year, according to survey results released Wednesday, extending a winning streak as record numbers of overseas visitors continue to flock to the country.
Japan took the top spot in the U.S. edition of the magazine Conde Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards for “Best Countries in the World.”
Italy ranked second, followed by Ireland, Cambodia and Spain.
The results demonstrate the country’s enduring appeal among international travelers as inbound tourism continues to surge . A record 42.7 million overseas visitors came to Japan in 2025, according to Justice Ministry figures.
Tokyo’s Haneda Airport was ranked the sixth best in the world, with Singapore’s Changi Airport taking the top place.
In a news release Wednesday, the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO) said Japan’s strong showing reflected not only the appeal of its tourism resources, but also qualities distinctive to Japan, such as its hospitality and safety.
“We hope that this continued international recognition will generate even greater interest in Japan and encourage more people to visit,” the organization wrote.
Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes in this year’s awards, the magazine’s 39th edition. The awards, held annually since 1988, rank destinations and travel experiences based on readers’ overall evaluations, with voting across categories including countries, hotels and cruises.
In the magazine’s U.K. edition of the rankings, Japan placed second behind Greece, with Italy, Turkey and Portugal completing the top five. The magazine highlighted the country’s restaurants, hot springs, cherry blossoms and high-speed rail network, as well as its mix of traditional culture, design and technological innovation.
“We will continue to showcase the unique attractions of regions across Japan, including their nature, culture, and cuisine, to audiences around the world, while encouraging travel to regional destinations and working toward sustainable tourism,” JNTO wrote.

articles.title_orig: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze
articles.title_zh: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze
articles.content_orig:
Russian officials said a Liberian-flagged tanker was attacked and a crew of 23 Indian nationals rescued
An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.
The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.
“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.
A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.
Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.
Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.
Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.
Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.
After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km) off Bulgaria’s coast, he said.
Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.
Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor ​Vitali ‌Klitschko said ‌on Telegram.
Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.
A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged ⁠an industrial facility, ​officials said, without giving details.
Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia strikes back after deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh and airports
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia strikes back after deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh and airports
articles.content_orig:
Houthi fighters seen in Yemen after militia group claims attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha, Saudi Arabia
Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom.
Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.
In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.
The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.
Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca.
Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added.
The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.
The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country.
Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".
The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.
But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.
In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".
The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".
The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.
The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

The laser-accessible nuclear transition in the thorium-229 isotope has been identified as a candidate for realizing an optical nuclear clock 1 that might outperform current optical clocks based on electron-shell transitions in atoms or ions 2 . It is expected to be more robust against external perturbations 3 , 4 and to provide enhanced sensitivity in clock-based tests of the fundamental principles of physics 5 , 6 . Here we realize a thorium-229 nuclear clock by stabilizing a continuous-wave laser to the 148-nm nuclear transition with rapid feedback based on absorption spectroscopy 7 . The thorium-229 nuclei are embedded in a millimetre-sized, room-temperature calcium fluoride crystal. A subharmonic of the 148-nm radiation is continuously compared with a Yb + single-ion clock. The nuclear clock shows a shot-noise-limited fractional frequency instability of \(3\times 1{0}^{-12}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) where τ is the averaging time, approaching 10 −15 instabilities over 1 day of operation. Improvements to the instability by several orders of magnitude are projected for future devices. We use the nuclear clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter by searching for periodic fluctuations and slow drifts in the nuclear transition energy, on timescales between 20 s and 1 day. Benefitting from the enhanced sensitivity of the thorium-229 transition, these constraints compete with the best atomic clocks concerning dark matter coupling to photons and go beyond previous measurements regarding coupling to the strong force.
Over the last 70 years, atomic clocks based on microwave and optical electronic transitions have successfully served as frequency standards based on their high levels of stability and accuracy 2 , 8 , 9 , 10 . To elevate these atomic timekeeping devices to the next generation, in 2003, Peik and Tamm 1 proposed a nuclear clock based on the extraordinarily low-energy isomeric state of the thorium-229 ( 229 Th) isotope at 8.4 eV. With a lifetime approaching 1 h for a bare nucleus in vacuum, this transition offers a potential resonance quality factor of the order of 10 19 (ref. 11 ). Additionally, the nucleus couples only weakly to perturbative fields 12 , which allows the construction of an optical clock implemented in a solid material at room temperature 13 . By doping microgram amounts of 229 Th into a crystal host, an experimentally simple and robust clock can be created, offering a large gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared with approaches based on a single or a few isolated nuclei, while only moderately degrading the resonance quality factor 1 , 4 , 11 , 14 .
A clock based on the 229 Th nuclear transition is of great interest for testing theories beyond the Standard Model of particle physics that indicate that the fundamental constants vary over time 5 . The low energy of the 229 Th isomer transition originates from a coincidental near-cancellation of the mega-electronvolt-scale Coulomb and nuclear contributions to the binding energies of the 229 Th ground and excited states, making the transition frequency highly sensitive to fluctuations in the coupling constants of the interactions involved 5 , 6 , 15 . As a result, a solid-state nuclear clock in its development phase would already be competitive with or may even surpass the sensitivity of advanced comparable atomic clocks in the search for dark matter.
The realization of a nuclear clock builds upon half a century of scientific discoveries. See the reviews in refs. 12 , 16 . In a research stream initiated by Kroger and Reich in 1976 (ref. 17 ), the energy of the 229 Th nuclear transition was narrowed down from an originally conjectured value of below 100 eV to −1(4) eV (ref. 18 ), 3.5(1.0) eV (ref. 19 ) and then 7.8(5) eV (refs. 20 , 21 ) using gamma spectroscopy. Using the internal conversion decay channel, the existence of the 229 Th isomer was proven in 2016 (ref. 22 ) and the energy value refined to 8.28(17) eV (ref. 23 ). An optical detection of the 229 Th radiative nuclear decay was realized in 2022, which determined the isomer energy to be 8.338(24) eV (ref. 24 ) in the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) range. Thereafter, resonant laser excitation in Th:CaF 2 , Th:LiSrAlF 6 crystals and ThF 4 and ThO 2 thin films was reported in 2024 and 2025 (refs. 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ), quickly followed by the resolution of the nuclear quadrupole structure in Th:CaF 2 (refs. 13 , 29 ).
The development of 148-nm continuous-wave laser systems in 2025 (refs. 30 , 31 ), in combination with highly doped 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 32 , 33 , has enabled the measurement of the nuclear transition with absorption spectroscopy 7 . With this technique, it became possible to probe the 229 Th nuclear transition continuously, without being limited by the long isomeric state lifetime of approximately 10 min. Moreover, absorption provides a higher detection efficiency, yielding three orders of magnitude more signal photons per second compared with fluorescence.
An optical clock is based on an atomic transition with a narrow linewidth, which is probed by a clock laser with a long coherence time. By stabilizing this laser to the atomic resonance, it can inherit the desired stability and reproducibility from the atom. Aiming for millihertz resolution and accuracy, the feedback times in this process typically extend to several seconds, requiring a pre-stabilization of the laser for higher-frequency noise to an optical cavity that has a suitable short-term stability. With the combination of these two control loops, very stable laser frequencies can be generated and then converted into a time signal through a frequency comb acting as an optical clockwork 34 .
Here, we transfer this concept from an atomic to a nuclear reference transition. Although previous studies 7 , 13 , 14 demonstrated that it is possible to excite the 229 Th nucleus using VUV lasers stabilized to external frequency standards, it has not yet been possible to construct a system in which the laser interrogating the 229 Th nuclei is steered by the nuclear transition itself. Our system is a nuclear clock that operates as a stand-alone device.
The nuclear clock is composed of a cavity-stabilized laser for short-term stability (referred to as the clock laser) and a 229 Th interrogation system providing long-term stability (Fig. 1a ). We use a continuous-wave VUV laser source to interrogate the 229 Th nuclei 7 , 30 . This laser source comprises a 1,187-nm frequency-quadrupled commercial laser (the seed laser in Fig. 1 ) and a single-pass second-harmonic-generation stage using a randomly quasi-phase-matched strontium tetraborate (SBO) crystal. The frequency and linewidth of the 1,187-nm interrogation laser are determined by an offset phase lock to the clock laser. We modulate the offset lock frequency to perform absorption measurements. For the clock laser, we use a high-finesse cavity-stabilized external-cavity diode laser operating at 1,187 nm. The stabilization of the clock laser to the cavity uses a Pound–Drever–Hall scheme on a sideband generated by an electro-optical modulator, allowing us to shift the frequency of the clock laser independently of the cavity resonances.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
articles.content_orig:
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena.
Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”
Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”.
The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats.
In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen.
“You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.”
Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections.
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support.
“Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.”
Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America,” and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.”
The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/ Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.
Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%.
Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run.
Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”
Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.”
The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of Republican governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump.
Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

articles.title_orig: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
articles.title_zh: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
articles.content_orig:
One of the seven men named in the lawsuit filed by a former Cornell University student who alleges that she was sexually assaulted at an on-campus fraternity house has filed a petition to block New York Attorney General Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor in the case .
The attorney for Gillio Lopes, who has denied that he sexually assaulted the woman, filed a petition in Albany County Supreme Court on Wednesday. His filing says James should not be the prosecutor in the case because she has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants named in the Civil Case.”
The Article 78 petition, filed against James and Gov. Kathy Hochul, is a proceeding used to challenge an action by a state or local government officer or agencies in New York.
Hochul appointed James last week to independently investigate Jane Doe’s allegations in the lawsuit, in which she says she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. In her role, James will determine whether criminal charges are warranted.
James’ office declined to comment on the Article 78 filing.
In a statement Monday, James said: “My office enforces our state’s laws to protect all New Yorkers. I am committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.”
Hochul’s office reiterated support for James on Wednesday.
Reached for comment on Lopes’ filing, the governor’s office referred to her comments last week.
“I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case,” Hochul said at the time.
Hochul appointed James after she expressed dismay over Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation of Doe’s allegations. He has said his office found a lack of criminality at the time and declined to press charges, but he reopened the case after the lawsuit sparked national uproar.
Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against Cornell, Chi Phi and seven fraternity brothers. None of the men named have been criminally charged.
The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.
Cornell said in a statement Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation in 2024 that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions ” from the university. Two of the fraternity members were expelled, and two others were suspended. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and required to write “reflection papers,” according to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation.
Lopes’ filing argues that James’ appointment is “improper” and cites a post her office shared on X on Sept. 28 , three days before her appointment was announced. In the post, she said: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”
The post, the petition contends, “made clear that she has formed an opinion about the case” and that “she has already reached the conclusion that Petitioner and the other named Defendants are guilty.”
The petition also seeks to have the court review James’ appointment and asks that her appointment be annulled or modified so she is not personally directing the probe or any resulting prosecution.
Stuart Bernstein, an attorney for Lopes, said Wednesday: “As Governor Hochul has said, the public needs confidence in the individual leading this investigation. AG James, based upon her very public statements validating Jane Doe, certainly doesn’t instill confidence in a fair investigation.”
In her lawsuit, Doe accuses Lopes of kissing her and sexually assaulting her without her consent.
Attorneys for two of the seven men, including Lopes, have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the other men.
On Tuesday, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney for Lopes, said he welcomes Cornell’s decision to have an independent review of its handling of Doe’s allegations, which will be led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates.
“In our experience, Cornell’s investigations have generally been thorough. That said, we have also seen due process problems that have affected respondents, and on at least two occasions we have gone to federal court to try to address those issues. In this case, we do not agree with the outcome as to Mr. Lopes,” Miltenberg said.

articles.title_orig: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.title_zh: World Health Organization says Russian lab worker’s death has not been clearly linked to plague
articles.content_orig:
Frank McGeorge, MD , Local 4's Medical Expert
The World Health Organization says Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the Irkutsk region.
The worker’s cause of death remains unclear.
A worker at a Siberian research institute that studies plague died after developing pneumonia, prompting officials to monitor and quarantine people who had contact with her and renewing questions about a disease many associate with the Middle Ages.
But Russian authorities have reported no plague cases in the region.
The World Health Organization said Russian officials described the worker’s illness as initially resembling a typical acute respiratory viral infection.
Officials have not publicly established the cause of death.
The worker died Oct. 2 at a hospital near Irkutsk, according to Reuters.
About 200 people who had contact with her were quarantined, and a local official said 60% had since been released.
Russian officials said no plague was found among the contacts who had been tested.
The WHO said it has been in contact with Russian authorities. Reports of the death have fueled speculation online, but Reuters reported there is no public evidence supporting the theories circulating on social media.
The incident has also revived memories of COVID-19.
But plague is not a new or unidentified disease. COVID-19 was caused by a newly identified virus; plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a well-studied bacterium that persists in animal populations in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Dr. Leonard Johnson said plague persists in animal populations and continues to cause sporadic human cases around the world, including in the United States.
The CDC has said there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States from the Russian case.
There are three main forms of plague.
Bubonic plague, the most common, typically follows the bite of an infected flea and causes swollen lymph nodes.
Septicemic plague affects the blood; both it and bubonic plague are generally acquired through infected fleas.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread through respiratory droplets from an infected person or animal, usually with close contact.
Pneumonic plague can be highly fatal if untreated, said Dr. Leonard Johnson, chief of infectious diseases at Henry Ford St. John Hospital.
But modern antibiotics can treat plague when given promptly. Johnson said people identified as close contacts of a confirmed case could be given preventive antibiotics, including doxycycline or ciprofloxacin, to reduce the chance of secondary infections.
He said the risk of wider spread remains low, particularly in the United States. That is a sharp contrast with the medieval epidemics that killed millions.
Experts remain cautious because they do not have direct access to the underlying information, and public statements by Russian authorities have not clearly established the cause of death.
So far, however, reports do not confirm plague or indicate a wider outbreak.

AEW Women’s World Champion Mercedes Moné got everything she could handle from Queen Aminata in front of a Parisian crowd that was fully behind Aminata’s quest to win her first AEW gold. All that and more went down on our first night in Paris!
The night began with the ROH World Championship on the line! Kofi, one third of the AEW World Trios Champions, made his way to the ring to a raucous ovation inside the Adidas Arena, accompanied by another third of the champions, Austin Creed.
The champion came out next, and he wasn't alone either — Bandido was flanked by Brody King for this championship tilt.
The referee called for the Code of Honor, and not only did both men shake hands, but they embraced. A hyped-up crowd was fully behind this matchup, which only fed the energy of both Kofi and Bandido.

When Kofi tried to dive to the outside, Bandido simply stepped out of the way, and Kofi's head bounced off the top rope. Bandido tried to climb back to the apron, but Kofi caught him with another dropkick, knocking him to the floor again. Kofi then charged and flipped over the top rope onto the floor, crushing Bandido, and took control of the early going.
Kofi rolled Bandido back into the ring and climbed the ropes. As Bandido got to his feet, Kofi leaped off the top for a cross body — but Bandido caught him in mid-air and, in an incredible display of strength, lifted him into a delayed vertical suplex, holding him aloft one-armed as the crowd counted all the way to twenty before finally dropping him to the mat.
The sheer exhaustion of that suplex left both men down. It was then that Swerve Strickland, the third member of the AEW World Trios Champions, made his way out with Prince Nana to join Creed in supporting Kofi. Only steps behind him, however, was “Hangman” Adam Page, and when Swerve spotted him, Creed and Nana had to hold him back. Page simply walked past and joined King at ringside to support their partner.
Bandido played to the crowd before turning his attention back to Kofi, landing a pair of corner strikes followed by a diving gut check that doubled Kofi over in pain. Bandido fired off more strikes in an adjacent corner, but when he went for a third, Kofi slipped away and whipped him to the opposite corner. With Bandido seated against the turnbuckle, Kofi drove a running knee into the side of his face, followed by elevated stomps to the chest. Kofi then ran in from the opposite corner for a shotgun dropkick, connecting flush. He covered, but Bandido kicked out to keep his title reign alive.

But when Kofi came up after him, Bandido turned it around with a gorilla press slam, dumping Kofi onto the top turnbuckle before following with a dropkick that put him on the mat! Bandido covered, but Kofi kicked out at two.
Bandido tried to whip Kofi across the ring, but Kofi reversed it with a kick to the stomach, then leaped for a leg drop to the back of Bandido's head. Kofi started building momentum, landing backhanded chops followed by a jumping side kick that put Bandido back down. Bandido avoided a follow-up jumping clothesline and whipped Kofi to the corner, but as he rushed in, Kofi flipped back with a pendulum kick through the ropes, then went up top for a frog splash cross body that got another near-fall.
Kofi bounced off the ropes for a jumping lariat, then fired up the Paris crowd before connecting with a Boom Drop. As Bandido stumbled to his feet, Kofi measured him for T.I.P., but Bandido ducked out of the way. Kofi spun him around in a rear waistlock and sent him to the corner. Bandido kicked his way out and leaped to the top rope for a reverse tornillo that got a two-count.
Bandido pushed Kofi into the ropes, but Kofi rebounded with a jumping spin kick to the head for another near-fall. The crowd roared as Bandido started to fight back, only for Kofi to cut him off with a kick to the gut. The two traded strikes off the ropes until Bandido popped Kofi up into a knee strike. As Bandido came off the ropes, Kofi leaped into the air and stomped him into the mat.
The crowd was fully invested as both men's partners continued to will them on from ringside. Bandido rose in the corner as Kofi waited in the opposite one; when Kofi charged in, Bandido met him with a kick combination and climbed to the second rope. As Bandido came off, Kofi caught him and rolled him through for an SOS into the second buckle! That’s a new and brutal variation on that move, matching Bandido's own escalating viciousness in this battle for championship gold.
As Creed and Swerve, along with the crowd, urged Kofi toward the top rope, he slowly made his way up. With Bandido doubled over below, Kofi leaped off and splashed him flat onto his back! That was an unorthodox execution, but even more devastating!  Bandido kicked out to preserve his reign!

articles.title_orig: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by Oct. 7, see only a threat
articles.title_zh: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by Oct. 7, see only a threat
articles.content_orig:
SDEROT, Israel — One by one, Israelis peered through the tourist-style binoculars at the shattered Gaza town of Beit Hanoun, a distance of several football fields away, where buildings tilted in the rubble like broken teeth. The only noticeable movement was dust kicked up by Israel’s military.
The Israelis squinted for a few moments and gestured others over. The lookout is a rare place where they can confront the Palestinian territory firsthand, and some celebrate its devastation.
An Israeli documentary released this year included one onlooker exclaiming, “Wow, destroyed beautifully.” The Associated Press heard similar sentiments there.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people in southern Israel and abducted 251 others, leading to a devastating war and, eventually, a fragile ceasefire.
Three years on, a visit to the communities attacked that day made clear: It’s too soon for many residents to see the Palestinians next door as anything other than a threat.
The highway running parallel to Gaza, where militants gunned down people trying to flee, is dotted with memorials. Victims’ smashed and bullet-pocked cars are assembled elsewhere, rusting and piled a half-dozen high. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a potential attack were disregarded, mark their deaths that day.
One resident, Deganit Bar Hay, said she still can’t barbecue because the smell of burnt flesh — “the smell of hell” — is a trigger.
Globally, there is shock and condemnation over how Israel has conducted the war, and how Gaza remains in ruins and cut off from the world a year since the ceasefire. Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and the vast majority of its 2 million residents live in rat-infested tent camps or among the debris.
But empathy for them is still unthinkable for many in Israel, with memories raw. Israeli media report little on the Palestinians of Gaza, and Israelis rarely if ever hear their voices unless they seek them out.
A new Israeli documentary, “NAZA,” in which military insiders describe what they said was the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has sparked outrage at the filmmakers, not the government. Everywhere in Israel — at train stations, beaches, the Gaza viewpoint — are dozens of stickers in memory of the hundreds of soldiers killed on Oct. 7 and in the ensuing war.
“We are post-traumatic, all of us,” said Ziporah Livneh, outside a cafe catering to tour groups and soldiers a short drive from Gaza. Much of her family died in the Holocaust, and she came to Israel at the age of 2.
Now, she said, the answer for Gaza is to keep believing in people’s humanity but respond strongly to acts of evil. A society and a country can’t be built on revenge, but for the world to think “we can be Mother Teresa, it is a hypocrisy.”
Many Israelis are still turned inward. They say their story isn’t being heard or understood. They assert that Palestinians in Gaza receive more attention, even as Israel’s government still prevents journalists from entering the territory except under rare, highly managed visits — and very few Palestinians can leave.
From the day the war began, Israeli news and hearts were focused on the dead and the hostages taken into Gaza, a land that despite being an hour’s drive from Tel Aviv has long felt remote. Cross-border contact had been severely limited since Hamas seized power in 2007. Then, on Oct. 7, militants ripped the fence apart.
This is the first anniversary since the attack that all remaining hostages are out of Gaza, alive or dead.
There is rebuilding in the Israeli communities where militants went home to home, burning and shooting. There is also the insistence on keeping Oct. 7 memories alive, with hope that the outside world will come to understand how Israel’s sense of security was smashed.
“I know many people around the globe don’t understand us,” said Mor Izreal, director of an Oct. 7 virtual reality exhibit in the border city of Sderot. She said over 10,000 people have visited since it opened a year and a half ago, most from overseas. Reactions range from sadness to rage to connectedness, she said.
This year, for the first time since the attack, there is also an election, a momentous and angry one.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is deeply divisive. Many Israelis accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7 attack and not securing the hostages’ release sooner, before many of them were killed. He is also accused of corruption and threatening democratic institutions.
But there has been little criticism of how his government has treated the Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel’s military now controls over 60% of the territory, squeezing them into an ever-smaller space.
Next to a bullet-pocked rocket shelter outside Sderot, a man held a banner calling for an official inquiry into the security failures surrounding the attack. Netanyahu has long resisted one.
Amit Gurfinkel said he spent Oct. 7 in a safe room with his daughter in the nearby community of Netivot, holding a knife and expecting the worst.
Gurfinkel is a minority in a population that has long supported Netanyahu. Posted across Sderot are campaign banners for his far-right allies, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir — the national security minister who has called for killing “30 to 40” people in targeted assassinations in Gaza each night.
Security is paramount, especially in Sderot, where residents have just 10 seconds to seek shelter when rockets are fired from Gaza. But Gurfinkel sees Israel’s reputation as crucial, too. He shook his head over passing drivers who shouted their support for Netanyahu, whose government is isolated over the destruction in Gaza and who has been issued an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court.
“This is pathological. I don’t know,” Gurfinkel said. “Sociologists and psychologists will have answers in the years to come.”
Some Israelis argue there are no real civilians among Palestinians in Gaza, pointing to Hamas’ entrenchment. Some Palestinians feel the same way about Israelis, noting that military service is mandatory for most Jewish men and women.
“Death to Arabs” is written inside a rocket shelter across from the Sderot police station that was besieged and then destroyed. “Hamas is still in Gaza” is scrawled on a guardrail on the highway where bodies spilled from vehicles on Oct. 7. “Make Gaza Jewish Again” is on a banner in a public square in Jerusalem’s Old City.
There is little public discussion about how everyday Palestinians are doing after three years of war.
“I think about them, and it’s complicated,” Adi Marmelstain said of the people in Gaza. She was visiting the sprawling memorial for the Nova music festival, where hundreds of people were shot dead on Oct. 7.
Her 20-year-old daughter, a member of the security forces like many young Israelis, stood in shorts and a tank top, her rifle slung across her. Both knew people who had been killed.
Marmelstain recalled waking up another daughter on Oct. 7 and sending her to war with bottled water and cookies. She later asked herself what she had been thinking. Three years later, life is not much easier to contemplate.
The world doesn’t see Israel in the right light, she said. And the Palestinians in Gaza?
“I think they have the right to live, but they choose not to,” she said.
Associated Press video journalist Alon Bernstein in Sderot, Israel, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
articles.title_zh: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
articles.content_orig:
MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.
Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

articles.title_orig: Russell calls world record, engagement a perfect close to 2026
articles.title_zh: Russell calls world record, engagement a perfect close to 2026
articles.content_orig:
LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Olympic champion Masai Russell said she knew she had the speed to break the 100-meter hurdles world record. She just did not know what it would feel like when it happened.
“When I ran the 12.09, I was just like, wow,” the former Kentucky athlete said in a sit-down interview with WKYT.
Russell clocked 12.09 seconds on Aug. 27 at the Diamond League meet in Zurich, Switzerland, shaving three-hundredths of a second off Tobi Amusan’s 12.12. The wind reading was 0.0 meters per second. Amusan, the previous record holder, finished second in 12.23. Nadine Visser was third in 12.34.
She closed the season by winning the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship, taking the 100-meter hurdles title Sept. 11 in Budapest in 12.22. Amusan was second again, in 12.34, and Visser third in 12.39.
The Zurich run was the centerpiece of a season in which Russell went unbeaten in Diamond League competition, winning all seven of her races and the Diamond Trophy. She is the reigning Olympic gold medalist from the Paris Games.
Russell said competition still pulls something different out of her. She said she studies athletes and performers who take on another persona in their field, naming Michael Jordan and LeBron James.
“I see what people say. I see the doubters. I see the haters,” she said. “I also see, of course, all the love that I get, too. So, you know, you see it all. But I think for me, I love proving people wrong.”
The world record has not changed the target. Russell said she wants to stay at the top of the podium every year.
“I just wanna continue every single year, just being one of those people that’s always at the top of the podium, that’s always winning, that’s always dominating, and really just, like, looking like the Usain Bolt of the women’s 100 hurdles,” she said.
The year has not been only about the track. Russell said she and longtime boyfriend Robbie Springfield, a former Kentucky athlete, are engaged. She announced the engagement last weekend.
“It’s just a beautiful way to top off such a great year, such a great season,” Russell said. “Robbie’s been a huge, huge, huge part of my success, like, on the track. So yeah, I mean, beautiful way to top off this 2026 season, no lie.”

articles.title_orig: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.title_zh: Mamdani draws bipartisan backlash for criticizing Israel on Oct. 7 anniversary
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- New York City marked the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack on Israel on Wednesday, a day that was filled with both anguish and anger from both sides of the ongoing conflict.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani faced criticism from multiple sides during a vigil in Union Square marking the attack that killed more than 1,200 Israeli civilians.
The event, described as a show of solidarity and resilience honoring those killed and remembering their pain, was marked by tension and confrontation. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators interrupted portions of the gathering, chanting: "It's not complicated! It's not complicated! Gaza will be liberated! Gaza will be liberated!"
Mamdani was met with chants of "traitor" and "sellout" and faced jeers from some attendees. The mayor, Public Advocate Jumaane Williams and former City Comptroller Brad Lander were criticized by some within their political base during efforts to promote unity.
Messages from the stage expressing sympathy for the 74,000 Palestinian lives lost in Gaza were met with opposition from some in attendance.
"If the Israeli army enters Rafa we may all die. Time is running out, the bombing continues, and no one has moved to save us yet. Thank you all for organizing this protest for innocent lives on both sides every week," one speaker said.
Williams addressed the competing grief surrounding the conflict.
"I'm trying to make sure I lift up the pain of everybody. I think too often people are trying to force people to choose. I'm not choosing. Theres a lot of pain. There's a lot of death. There's a lot of innocent people who lost their lives," he said.
Earlier Wednesday, NewsCopter 7 observed pro-Palestinian demonstrators marching from City Hall, where flags were flying at half-staff. Students at Columbia University also staged a walkout.
In Gravesend, Brooklyn, some New York City councilmembers called for a permanent memorial at the Mickey Kairey Garden to honor those who were killed and those who were taken hostage on Oct. 7, 2023. The memorial would occupy a 6-by-6-foot footprint and would become what supporters say is the first public memorial of its kind in the city. Supporters say it would provide a permanent space to remember those who were murdered and taken hostage, while educating future generations so the atrocities are never forgotten.
In Tenafly, New Jersey, the family of former hostage Edan Alexander joined Rep. Josh Gottheimer to announce legislation aimed at helping survivors, victims and families.
Meanwhile, the mayor drew additional criticism after releasing an Oct. 7 statement earlier Wednesday. In the statement, he described the anniversary as "profoundly painful."
"We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day," the statement said in part.
The statement also described Israel's response in Gaza as an "ongoing genocide," condemned U.S. military support for Israel and added that "we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue."
The post prompted backlash from Jewish organizations, including the Anti-Defamation League, marking the latest development in the mayor's complex and often tense relationship with New York's Jewish population.
"The city with the largest population of Jews outside of Israel, deserves a mayor who can mourn their dead with them without engaging in such political grandstanding," the Anti-Defamation League said in a statement.
The New York Board of Rabbis also criticized the statement.
"This is a day of mourning for us. Just give us that day. We can have all the other discussions, debates, on different days. But don't do it today," Rabbi Joe Potasnik said.
Mamdani campaigned as a strong defender of Palestinian rights. As mayor, he has sought to balance that position while also participating in Jewish holiday observances.
He did not make any public remarks during Tuesday's vigil.
