articles.title_orig: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died in hospital
articles.title_zh: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died in hospital
articles.content_orig:
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol - a square in Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing - with a collective gasp followed by a minute of silence.
Dozens of candles were lit around the square while more candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then marched from Puerta del Sol to the Spanish Congress, chanting "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
One protester told the BBC that people would remain in the square "as long as necessary".
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week .
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences and wrote on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.

articles.title_zh: The World Figure and Fancy Skating Championships return to Lake Placid
articles.content_orig:
The World Figure and Fancy Skating Championships are back in Lake Placid this weekend.
The Olympic sport combines figure skating with artistic expression, while it uses a unique canvas.
Skaters create artistic designs on the ice with their blades and technique.
Ice is painted black making way for the art to be created and seen.
Skating legends from the past and current professionals come together to create different patterns on the ice.
This year, the performances will include something the world championships have never seen before.
"This year there is a live improvisation to live musicians of which you're going to see skaters and performers, world class performers who've never actually skated the routine before at that moment in front of the audience," said Karen Courtland Kelly, a former U.S. Olympian and Chef De Mission of the World Figure Sports Society. "It's never been done in a World championship, but we're going to do it for the first time ever in Lake Placid with live improvisation to live music."
The championships start Thursday, Oct. 8, and wrap up on Sunday, Oct. 11.

articles.title_orig: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
articles.title_zh: World must change way it produces food to avoid biodiversity collapse, says WWF
articles.content_orig:
A landmark report reveals that the world must change the way it produces food to avoid a biodiversity collapse
Conservation comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and green​ sea turtles prove that global nature loss can be reversed, ​scientists have said. ​But a report warns food production must be the next ​“positive tipping point​” if the world is to avert biodiversity collapse.
The World Wildlife Fund ( WWF ) analysed nearly 36,000 animal populations and more than 5,000 species, producing the largest ever database of vertebrate wildlife. Scientists found populations had declined by an average of 73% since 1970, showing that “nature continues to be degraded at an alarming scale”, with “no sign of losses slowing”.
Nature loss is no longer just an environmental challenge but a direct threat to the global economy, the report says, noting that about half of global GDP – roughly $58tn (£44tn) in 2023 – depends on nature and its ecosystem services. The authors write that species collapse now poses an “existential threat to economic stability, geopolitical security and human wellbeing”.
Animal populations were found to be falling most sharply in tropical, biodiversity-rich regions, while trends in northern temperate parts of the world appeared much gentler.
In Latin America and the Caribbean, land and freshwater wildlife populations fell by an average of 95% between 1970 and 2022, while the equivalent declines were 80% in Africa and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
Freshwater wildlife suffered the sharpest losses across the world’s ecosystems, with monitored populations in rivers and lakes down by an average of 85%, compared with 69% for land species and 59% for marine species.
Tanya Steele, the chief executive of WWF UK, said: “Nature loss is not just a crisis for wildlife. It’s already sending us the bill through growing risks to our food security, water supplies, economy and resilience to climate shocks.
“We stand at a fork in the road: either we continue paying the rising price of nature loss, or we invest in nature’s recovery and a future where people and wildlife can thrive together.”
But despite the pattern of global biodiversity decline, wild tigers, green sea turtles and bluefin tuna are recovering, the report said, showing that “it is still possible to reverse the global loss of nature when action is taken”.
In 2010, about 3,200 wild tigers remained globally and the species was sliding toward extinction. After sustained and targeted conservation interventions, the population has grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%.
Becci Day, WWF UK’s tiger lead, said the remarkable comeback of wild tigers demonstrated the “science of hope” and proved that when climate and ecological action was taken, change was possible.
The report said Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna populations, which were collapsing after decades of overfishing, had now recovered to the point where neither was now considered threatened.
Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever downlisted from endangered to “least concern” on the IUCN red list, reflecting 50 years of coordinated conservation work across about 80 countries.
Dr Mike Barrett, the chief scientific adviser for WWF UK and a co-author of the report, said: “These are examples that show that nature can recover even when pushed right to the brink, and they provide us with inspiration. It’s also very clear that conservation alone cannot tackle the scale of threats facing nature.”
He said nature would have no chance of recovery if “negative tipping points ” – self-reinforcing, irreversible ecological changes that accelerate climate crisis – were passed. “The systems which drive nature’s loss have to be transformed. And that’s energy, food and finance,” he said.
“Our report shows that we’ve already passed the tipping point in the energy sector with the take-up of renewable energy . That transition is now unstoppable. It’s not happening fast enough, but it is unstoppable.”
Humanity must likewise adapt the way it produces food, he said. “Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and therefore the loss of biodiversity. It’s also a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and so helps drive climate change, so you have that feedback.”
Dr Steve Smith, a research fellow at Global Systems Institute and a co-author of the report, said: “The biggest prize for nature recovery would be a sustainable and healthy food system, but it’s currently the farthest away from positively tipping. For example, agricultural expansion drives almost 90% of deforestation worldwide.”
Positive tipping points are thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling.

articles.title_orig: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.title_zh: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.

UW–Madison has been named the top volunteer-producing university since 2017.
“Best Value Schools” ranking also jumps 23 spots, placing UW–Madison 24th in the nation.
The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.title_zh: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.content_orig:
After 58 years, Fuller Bazer, Ph.D., a University Distinguished Professor in the Texas A&M College of Agriculture and Life Sciences Department of Animal Science , will close out his scientific career in October.
During his groundbreaking tenure, Bazer also held joint appointments in the College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences Departments of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences and Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology ,
“Dr. Bazer has built an enduring legacy as one of the foremost reproductive scientists in the world,” said Clay Mathis, Ph.D., head of the Department of Animal Science, “Dr. Bazer may be retiring, but his innovative work that transformed our understanding of pregnancy establishment in livestock will continue to have an impact on the industry for many years to come.”
Bazer is a Regents Fellow, Distinguished Professor, Presidential Impact Fellow, and the O.D. Butler Chair in Physiology of Reproduction, as well as a top researcher in the world in the “Animal Science and Veterinary” category, as named by Research.com .
At 88, he is ranked, according to Google Scholar, as the most highly cited researcher in the field of reproductive biology. He is credited with discovering uteroferrin, a phosphatase, produced in response to progesterone that transfers iron to the developing embryo and stimulates red blood cell development. He also identified estradiol as the pregnancy recognition signal in swine and interferon tau as the signal in ruminants — findings that have reshaped animal management practices to improve pregnancy outcomes.
Those findings were published across 58 years, from 1968 to 2025, averaging 16.9 papers a year, with 46 of the 982 publications appearing in the last two years.
Bazer earned his bachelor’s in biology from Centenary College of Louisiana, his master’s in animal science from Louisiana State University and his doctorate in animal science from North Carolina State University. He was a member of the Department of Animal Science, University of Florida from October 1968 to 1992 before joining the Texas A&M Department of Animal Science on May 1, 1992.
In addition to maintaining highly productive research and teaching programs, Bazer served as director of the Center for Animal Biotechnology and Genomics, 1992–2001; director of the Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M University and Texas A&M Health Sciences Center, Texas Medical Center, Houston, 1994-2001; the inaugural vice president for research and interim dean of the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, January 1999 to December 2000, Texas A&M University System Health Science Center.
He also served as the associate vice chancellor and associate director of the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station, and executive associate dean of the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, January  2001 to December  2004; associate vice president for research, January 2005–December 2008; interim department head, Department of Veterinary Pathobiology, May-February 2010; and the World Class University Professor, Biomodulation Major, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea, March 1, 2010 to Aug. 31, 2013.
Bazer has had an outstanding career and significant impact on livestock fertility and reproduction, signified by his recognition as the recipient of the 2003 Wolf Prize in Agriculture for his interferon tau discovery as well as his discovery of other pregnancy-associated proteins. Additionally, he received the Alexander von Humboldt Award in Research in 2000. These are two of the highest awards in the field of agricultural sciences.
Bazer is also past recipient of the highest awards from each of his scientific societies: the Carl Hartman Award from the Society for the Study of Reproduction in 2004, the Morrison Award from the American Society of Animal Science in 2014, and the Marshall Medal from the Society for Reproduction and Fertility in 2025. He is also a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a recipient of the L.E. Casida Award for Graduate Education and the Animal Physiology and Endocrinology Award, both from the American Society of Animal Science. He earned awards for research, graduate education and service from the Society for the Study of Reproduction.

articles.title_zh: Army Sets Date for First Military Execution by Firing Squad Since 1945

A memorial to the victims of the Fort Hood shooting, pictured in November 2009, outside the apartment complex where Hasan lived. Eli Kaplan/Getty Images hide caption
President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan , the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.
But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.
"The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."
For example, Ronald Gray , who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.
It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.
"For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."
The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.
In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."
"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill , at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had " switched sides " and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.
The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.
Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center . They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/Bell County Sheriff's Department hide caption
The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.
" On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."
The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.
"They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013 . He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.
Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.
"We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.
The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.
"The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."
Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.
Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.
"The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."
The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May .
This photo provided by the South Carolina Department of Corrections shows the state's death chamber in Columbia, S.C., including the electric chair, right, and a firing squad chair, left. AP/South Carolina Department of Corrections hide caption
Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.
Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.
The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.
Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.

Disney Cruise Line will invite guests on a journey inspired by courageous Disney characters who believe in themselves, in their dreams, and in the promise and possibility of new horizons when the fleet’s new ship, the Disney Believe, sets sail December 18, 2027, from Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale, Fla.
The Disney Believe will introduce brand-new, can’t-miss experiences, including the world’s first stage adaptation of Walt Disney Animation Studios Encanto , a family dining venue that expands the Frozen universe with an all-new setting and experience, a Grand Hall inspired by the vibrant world where the sky meets the sea from Moana, and more.
The Disney Believe will offer four- and five-night sailings from south Florida to the Caribbean and The Bahamas, making stops at one or both of Disney Cruise Line’s island destinations, Disney Castaway Cay and Disney Lookout Cay at Lighthouse Point. Continuing Disney Cruise Line’s unprecedented growth which will see the fleet expand to 13 ships in late 2030, Disney Believe will be the fourth in the Wish class, joining its sister ships Disney Wish, Disney Treasure, and Disney Destiny.
The Grand Hall, the Disney Believe’s central gathering space, will embrace the spirit of exploration and the power of nature with an architectural meeting of the sky and sea as a statue of Moana, along with her trusty companions Pua and Heihei, guide visitors on their upcoming voyage. This heart of the ship will incorporate influences from the film’s Pacific Islands setting and design elements inspired by the sea itself, including an ocean-hued carpet adorned with bioluminescent colors and a chandelier modeled after the sea’s fluid movement with the heart of Te Fiti hidden within.
The Disney Believe will blend brand-new entertainment offerings from the worlds of Encanto and Zootopia with classic Disney Cruise Line experiences, bringing families into beloved stories and worlds, all with that signature Disney touch.
“Disney Encanto” will debut exclusively on the Disney Believe, adapting the Academy Award-winning Walt Disney Animation Studios film for the Walt Disney Theatre stage. Following Mirabel on a quest to save her loved ones and their miraculous home, this production is inspired by diverse Colombian cultures with vibrant costuming, creative scenic design and joyful, traditional dance styles, along with Disney Legend Lin-Manuel Miranda’s hits from the movie like “We Don’t Talk About Bruno” and “Surface Pressure.”
A hit show from the Disney Magic, “Tangled: The Musical” joins the theatrical lineup on the Disney Believe with a reimagined set design and special effects exclusive to the new ship. “Disney Seas the Adventure,” an original show for the Wish class featuring beloved Disney and Pixar characters and iconic songs, rounds out the Broadway-style shows coming to the Disney Believe.
Beyond the Walt Disney Theatre, guests will discover Gazelle , an entertainment hub inspired by the bustling metropolis from Disney Animation’s Zootopia films. By day, this location will be home to a variety of fun for families, such as trivia, games and immersive character encounters, but as nighttime comes around, cruisers can try everything with adult-exclusive entertainment, silent discos and variety acts. And for the first time onboard Disney Cruise Line, Judy Hopps and Nick Wilde from Zootopia will star in a new family show that will ask guests to help them solve their latest case.
Additionally, the Disney Believe will spotlight several fan-favorite entertainment experiences the whole family can enjoy:
Aboard the Disney Believe, a brand-new restaurant will bring the family together for dinner, joining two returning venues from the Wish class.
While on the Disney Believe, adults will be able to enjoy venues, offerings and entertainment tailored just for them, offering a delightful mix of fun and relaxation. Several of the bars and lounges on the Disney Believe will feature brand-new designs and menus inspired by the powerful stories that ignite imaginations and quench curiosity, all with a touch of sophistication.
At Sea Notes , guests will venture into an iridescent piano lounge inspired by Ariel’s grotto. Here, chic, contemporary design blends with whimsical artistry from the beloved Disney Animation film, The Little Mermaid . The centerpiece of the space is an elegant pearlescent piano, one of the forgotten treasures from Ariel’s secret grotto. Patrons will enjoy nostalgic melodies while sipping from an expertly crafted menu of dreamy cocktails and non-alcoholic beverages.
Adults will step into a vintage storybook at Wishing Well , a centrally located gathering space taking cues from Disney Animation’s 1937 film Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs . Guests will be invited into an enchanting castle courtyard under a canopy of white blossoms and red apples, with furnishings draped in the bold colors of Snow White’s gown, and hand-carved wood framing on the stage that will nod to the Seven Dwarfs cottage. The ornate bar, featuring a beautiful stained glass art piece, will evoke a gothic castle. Throughout the sailing, the lounge will host a variety of activities and feature live musical performances to enjoy while serving up a selection of mocktails, cocktails, spirits, and coffees.
Skygazers will be a venue where time stands still. Within this magical observatory-themed pub, dreamers and wish-makers will gather beneath the story-filled evening sky. Towering bookshelves, astronomical instruments and celestial maps, including props and nods to classic Disney stories, will adorn the walls of this astronomer’s laboratory. Whether viewing live sports broadcasts or pondering dreams, guests will sample from a thematic menu of custom-made craft brews, specialty cocktails and light bites.
Returning to the Disney Believe is the popular Disney Cruise Line experience, the Haunted Mansion Parlor , a fully immersive bar inspired by the iconic Disney Parks attraction. Foolish mortals will be welcomed to sip on an all-new menu of spirited craft cocktails and mocktails developed exclusively for the Disney Believe. Aboard the ship, additional adult-exclusive venues will include:
Like on its sister ships, the upper decks on the Disney Believe will feature three distinctly themed districts where cruisers can enjoy fun water features, quick and casual dining options, and ample areas to relax while they soak up the sun.
Within the family district themed to Mickey and Friends , families can take a dip in one of the seven pools scattered across tiered decks or relax in one of the many lounge chairs in and out of the sun, all while watching Disney films, live sports and more on the jumbo screen.
Disney Cruise Line’s signature attraction at sea, the AquaMouse , will also make its return. This 760-foot-long water ride brings its riders into a Mickey Mouse animated short. Aboard the Disney Believe, the AquaMouse will feature Mickey and Minnie Mouse as they embark on zany “Port Adventures”. From dashing up a snowy mountain slope on “Swiss Meltdown” to partaking in the villainous hijinks of “Sing a Silly Song,” there will be plenty of splashtacular surprises in store.
A water wonderland themed to Disney and Pixar’s Toy Story awaits for little cruisers. This area, designed specifically for families with toddlers and young children, will feature a themed splash zone, wading pool, family waterslide, and a smoothie bar.
Children will make their own vacation dreams come true aboard the Disney Believe. Within each of the dedicated spaces for kids ages 3 to 17, young cruisers can let their imagination run wild with programming facilitated with the care and expertise of Disney-trained counselors and special playtime with Disney character friends.

articles.title_orig: USS Lincoln nearly home after more than 300 days at sea
articles.title_zh: USS Lincoln nearly home after more than 300 days at sea
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE USS LINCOLN IN THE PACIFIC OCEAN — After spending more than 300 days at sea, service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will finally return home this week.
The beleaguered aircraft carrier with about 7,500 personnel is scheduled to dock Thursday in San Diego, amid sharp criticism over its prolonged deployment in the Middle East.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth acknowledged to crewmembers on Wednesday that he was the “only thing standing between you and home” and that he had been the one “who signed that orders book twice” to extend the ship’s deployment.
On Wednesday, the evening before they were set to dock, the mood seemed far more jovial aboard the ship; sailors were chatting and laughing, some were running a 5K around a deck now free of aircraft. A band played in the setting sun.
Navy reports eight suicide attempts on USS Lincoln
The Lincoln left San Diego in November and was initially expected to return before the summer months. Its deployment was extended after the Iran war began in February. The ship was at sea without a port of call for 286 days until early September, when it docked in Thailand for a handful of days. By that point, family members of those on board had raised concerns about dwindling food supplies and low morale.
At least eight service members attempted suicide during the many months at sea, according to a letter sent last month to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., by a top Navy official. The letter, obtained by NBC News , prompted concerns about the impact to mental health that such a lengthy deployment can have on service members. No deaths on the ship have been attributed to suicide.
Some family members of those on the ship said the extended time at sea was “wreaking havoc” on sailors’ mental health, and one described it as a “scene out of the ‘American Horror Story’” television show.
“Where he had been very positive, he started getting very dark,” one woman told NBC News about her son’s time at sea. Another parent said that she and her daughter, who is serving aboard the ship, grew increasingly frustrated as the Trump administration continued to push back the ship’s arrival date.
According to U.S. officials, a sailor assigned to the air wing on the Lincoln went overboard in early August and was quickly rescued and treated. That sailor was transferred off the ship for further medical care, the official told NBC News .
Navy officials initially said leadership had not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship.
According to the letter, suicide attempts occurred among crewmembers and sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Alicia Victoria Lozano is a California-based reporter for NBC News focusing on climate change, wildfires and the changing politics of drug laws.

articles.content_orig:
Masters of subtlety and destructive power take center stage in this World of Warcraft: Forever class deep dive. Discover how Rogues and Warlocks are evolving through updates that build on the defining tools, tactics, and playstyles of each class.
For Rogues, the update builds on their mastery of Stealth, control, Poisons, and precise weapon attacks. Poisons gain more charges and can be used alongside temporary weapon enchantments, while updates across Assassination, Combat, and Subtlety create stronger options for daggers, other weapon types, Finishing Moves, Bleeds, and combat tricks.
For Warlocks, the focus is on opening new ways to command Shadow, Fire, and demonic power. Banes separate damaging effects from utility Curses, pets scale with their master’s stats, and revised Firestones and Spellstones strengthen spell-focused weapon imbues. Talent updates across Affliction, Demonology, and Destruction further support damage-over-time and draining effects, deeper demon synergies, and distinct Shadow and Fire combinations.
Talents become available starting at level 10 and continue using a familiar structure, including one-point milestone talents at 11, 21, and 31 points, now joined by a new 16-point milestone. To change your talents, including Legacy talents, visit a class trainer in one of the major cities. Dual Specialization also becomes available at level 40.
Please note that class abilities and talents may continue to evolve throughout the beta test and are subject to additional changes.
Rogues excel at creating opportunities and turning them into decisive advantages. These updates give them more ways to prepare for an encounter, adapt once combat begins, and shape a build around the methods that suit them best.
Removed talents : Dagger Specializaton , Mace Specialization , Sword Specialization , Fist Weapon Specialization have all been subsumed into the new talent Hack and Slash.
Removed talents : Sleight of Hand, Deadliness.
Rogues remain the masters of Stealth , with unique abilities useable from Stealth like Pickpocket , Distract , Sap , and Garrote . They alone have access to Poisons and can now use them alongside temporary weapon enchantments. However, different varieties of Rogues specialize in different weapons and tactics. Assassination specializes in daggers and buffing themselves with Finishing moves.  Combat and Subtlety have support for all weapon types, with Combat focusing on hard hitting direct damage and little bit of cleave damage with Blade Flurry , and Subtlety focusing on combat tricks and Bleeds. Whichever specialization they choose, Rogues are welcome in any party or raid for their Stealth and control abilities, as well as the highest potential single-target melee damage in the game.
Warlocks bend forbidden powers to their will, turning every resource—from lingering afflictions to bound demons—into another means of defeating their enemies. These updates broaden how they manage those powers and create new connections among their spells, pets, and specialized tools.
Removed talents: Improved Curse of Weakness, Improved Drain Life, Improved Drain Mana, Improved Curse of Exhaustion, Grim Reach, Dark Pact.
Removed talents : Improved Healthstone, Fel Intellect, Fel Stamina, Improved Subjugate Demon, Improved Firestone, Improved Spellstone.
Removed talents :  Improved Firebolt, Improved Lash of Pain, Devastation, Improved Immolate, Emberstorm.
Warlocks are gaining new exciting combat options for WoW: Forever. With Affliction, they can concentrate on damage-over-time and draining effects, now with full viability from dealing critical strikes and competitive damage, and with the ability to sustain their own health via powerful health draining effects. With Demonology, they can specialize in empowering themselves and their pet in all new ways with Demonic Brand , Demonic Knowledge , and Demonic Pact , keeping foes focused on their pet while they decimate the enemy with Soul Fire . And with Destruction, they can now mix powerful Shadowburns and Conflagrates with the new Incinerate spell, and the new Bane of Havoc allowing them to continue damage on a primary target while dealing with lesser foes. Warlocks are still physically weak themselves, depending on their demon pets for protection, but they now do damage to compete with any other spellcaster, with three completely different styles to conduct that competition.
Whether striking from the shadows or wielding forbidden power, Rogues and Warlocks offer distinct ways to approach every encounter. Explore their updated talents, experiment with new combinations, and find the tactics that best suit your path through World of Warcraft: Forever .

President Donald Trump says he is seeking more answers about the death of a Russian worker from plague at a Siberian lab , a case that has ignited public health concerns worldwide.
During an Oval Office event Wednesday, the president was asked by Fox News if the death was the result of “a bioweapon.”
“Well, we don't think so,” Trump said. “We’re gonna find out soon enough, but we don’t think so, and if you listen to them, it's under control.”
“We've heard this before, a couple of years ago during your first term,” Fox reporter Peter Doocy then asked. “Are you getting the same vibe right now from Russia that you got from China at the start of Covid?”
“Well China didn’t say much, and Russia's not saying much either, but they do say they have it very much under control,” Trump said. He added that he plans to call Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day Wednesday, noting it is Putin’s birthday.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia , died Friday from pneumonia of an unknown cause. Authorities subsequently quarantined about 200 people.
Most have since been released, and Russian officials said no plague cases had been detected among Shipilova’s contacts. Officials also said she had been vaccinated and was “immune to ​the dangerous infections with which she worked,” adding there was no risk of an epidemic.
Global health officials have closely monitored the case and called for greater transparency, citing concerns about parallels to the early days of the Covid pandemic, which began with a small number of fatal respiratory illnesses.
World Health Organization chief Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday that a “full risk assessment” has not yet been possible.
He added that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Erica Schwartz said the agency is prepared to screen travelers, though she described the risk to Americans as very low.
The U.S. State Department also warned Moscow this week that its failure to disclose details about Shipilova’s death violated international health obligations, The Wall Street Journal reported.
“Plague infections occur regularly with a few hundred cases a year globally,” Paul Hunter, a professor of medicine at the University of East Anglia, previously told The Independent .
“There are different forms of the disease, bubonic and septicaemic are spread by flea bites from close contact with infected animals,” Hunter said. “Pneumonic plague is spread person to person through respiratory droplets.”

For the first time, World Girls Hockey Weekend is coming to the Roaring Fork Valley, giving girls and women a chance to hit the ice in Carbondale with no registration, fees or equipment required.
Colorado Extreme, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding hockey access in the Roaring Fork Valley, will host the free event at 5 p.m. Oct. 17 at the Steadman Philippon Outdoor Arena in Carbondale.
The event invites women of all ages in the Roaring Fork Valley, whether a seasoned skater or completely new to the sport, to come together and celebrate women’s hockey.
Colorado Extreme will provide free equipment to those who need it. Participants can bring a stick and play with friends, practice their skills or simply learn how to skate.
In addition to the free skate, Colorado Extreme will host a watch party with pizza for professional women’s hockey games.
No registration is required for the event.
World Girls Hockey Weekend is a global event that began in 2011. This year marks the first time the event has come to the Roaring Fork Valley as Colorado Extreme continues its mission to expand hockey opportunities for girls in the region.
“The biggest thing is just we’re trying to grow the girls’ game,” said Maddy Moses, a high-performance coach at Colorado Extreme.
Moses grew up playing hockey on the East Coast, where she said girls-only hockey programs were much more common.
“I grew up on the East Coast, so girls’ hockey is extremely prominent, and there’s so many opportunities,” Moses said. “That’s just not the case out west, and I feel like Colorado is getting on board with that finally, and giving girls opportunities to learn to play and to skate and to do it together, rather than just being a handful of girls on a boys’ team.”
Colorado Extreme has made accessibility a central part of its efforts to introduce more girls to the sport.
“It’s a really great place for young athletes that haven’t maybe experienced the sport to come to specifically Colorado Extreme and just try it,” Moses said. “I mean, it’s pretty unheard of that you go somewhere and you get completely free equipment and you get to get on the ice and you get to try it on multiple occasions.”
That same approach will carry into World Girls Hockey Weekend.
“No registration, no fees, nothing. Just show up. If you have gear, bring it. If you don’t have gear, we can get you some gear and get you out on the ice,” Moses said.

articles.title_zh: Georgia vs. Alabama weather tracker: SEC officials expect game to be played on time despite messy forecast
articles.content_orig:
It seems like the entire world will be descending upon Tuscaloosa this weekend, including Tropical Storm Isaias. The storm -- which is expected to bring heavy rains and possible flooding -- could impact this weekend's marquee showdown between No. 2 Georgia and No. 6 Alabama .
Despite speculation that the storm could move the game to a different day or location, the Crimson Tide and Bulldogs plan on playing in Bryant-Denny Stadium this Saturday, CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reports. It's possible the kickoff time could shift, but the current plan is to play as scheduled.
Earlier this week, an SEC spokesperson told CBS Sports that the conference is "keeping an eye on forecasts and staying in communication with schools with games that could be impacted by weather."
The storm is expected to bring locally heavy rain, potential flooding and high winds throughout the Southeast this weekend, although the exact path and timing is unknown. With that in mind, Alabama released a statement on Tuesday saying that there are currently "no plans to alter the contest."
As things stand at the moment, the forecast is calling for a good deal of rain and wind in Tuscaloosa on Saturday, but the conditions could be playable.
During their SEC teleconference, Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer and Georgia coach Kirby Smart both addressed the possibility of Tropical Storm Isaias affecting the game.
Smart said it's hard to simulate tropical storm conditions in practice. Neither Georgia nor Alabama can import a special effects department from Hollywood to create a monsoon on the practice field, but players can learn from how teams have managed messy conditions in the past.
"It's uncertainty. [It's] beyond my control," Smart said, per 247Sports . "We as coaches game plan for multiple situations - weather conditions - when they're there. We had that same prep last week with the threat of those things. Doesn't change a lot about practice. You have to practice good on good. You've got to practice for the long term of the season, not just for one week.
"You can't really practice conditions. You can't simulate them, so you're much better off to educate, learn from the past of other people who have played in them, and prepare your team to play and not make it about that."
DeBoer shared Smart's sentiment, saying there's little that can be done other than preparing as usual. The Crimson Tide will implement wet-ball drills for the second week in a row after prepping for rainy conditions ahead of last weekend's win over Mississippi State .
"Depends on the level of weather you get, it would affect what happens," DeBoer said, according to 247Sports . "It's just -- that's not my area of expertise. I'm just getting our football team ready. It hasn't affected us much, other than we're doing wet ball drills and get wet ball involved in some of our team reps, just like we did last week at times, preparing for the rain a week ago. I'm not really involved in too much."

articles.title_zh: Lone Jack teen Jax Cromwell carries US flag at Beach Wrestling World Championships
articles.content_orig:
LONE JACK, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Tod Palmer covers sports business and eastern Jackson County, including Independence. Share your story idea with Tod .
Lone Jack isn’t anywhere near a beach, but that didn’t stop Jax Cromwell, a 2025 Mules graduate , from becoming a rising star for USA Wrestling’s Beach Wrestling Team during the last year, giving him a chance to see the world.
"One of my biggest dreams actually is to travel the world, so to do it through the sport I love is just amazing," Cromwell said.
Cromwell, 19, competed last month at the 2026 Beach Wrestling World Championships in Katerini, Greece, where he was chosen as the U.S. team's flag bearer.
He competes in the USA Beach Wrestling 90+ kilogram division, both as a U-20 athlete and in regular events.
“Never in a million years would I think a kid from a small town in Missouri would ever be able to get to do something like that, so I'm definitely blessed and honored to be able to represent our country in that way,” Cromwell said. “... It was just an amazing honor.”
While Lone Jack is a long way from the beach, it is where Cromwell grew to love wrestling. His high school coach, Ben Call, recalled recognizing Cromwell's potential early after he decided not to play basketball in high school.
"Big kid, very athletic — got him out into some open mats, and then the rest is basically history after that," Call said.
Cromwell discovered beach wrestling through a teammate at Doane College in Nebraska last year and it was a breath of fresh air.
“All my life wrestling, I've always thought about the success,” he said. “I've always been fixated on winning and the outcome. When it came to this, it was just fun. I loved it. I did it because it made me happy, and I think that's the switch that flipped in my head and why I became so successful in it. It actually made me happy, so I just picked it up and ran with it.”
Cromwell said the experience in Greece — which he noted was the birthplace of wrestling, the world’s oldest sport — went beyond the competition itself.
"Even apart from the wrestling, it was definitely a breathtaking experience,” he said. “Something you know I'll never forget.”
Call said watching Cromwell grow from a freshman to a world championships competitor has been deeply rewarding.
"There were definitely moments that we've shared with him being a high school kid and getting into a little bit of things here and there, but he trusted me. ... I never gave up on him, and he never gave up on me being a coach to him and leading him the right direction, the right path. Just seeing the growth, from where he came in as a freshman and now being able to travel over to Greece, gave me so much joy. That's basically a boy becoming a man.”
It sets an incredible example for other Mules wrestlers, which he now helps coach, and kids in the Lone Jack community.
"The opportunities that are out there for these kids that are from Lone Jack and are so in this fishbowl, they don't get to see the outside world and understand, ‘Hey, there are tons of opportunities out there. You just have to be willing to go take them,’” said Call, who has coached the Mules boys wrestling team for a decade and will transition exclusively to coaching the girls team this winter.
Cromwell isn’t finished either. In fact, he’s just getting started.
“I actually got some recent news from my (USA Wrestling) coaches that they're going to be taking me on the World Series in 2027,” Cromwell said. “I'm going to spend the entire year traveling the world. I'm going to go to every single stop in the World Series. There will be five stops, as well as the Pan American Championships in Peru.”
Between meets, Cromwell has been invited to train with other USA Wrestling athletes, several Kansas and Missouri area colleges and even with teams in Europe.
Cromwell said beach wrestling is a fast-paced version of the sport, complicated by fighting for traction inside the sandy circle used for matches.
Opponents score a point anytime they get an opponent to touch anything other than a hand or foot to the ground. The first to three points wins.
"The match can end in 5 seconds with a three-point throw, feet to back, right," Cromwell said. "You get taken down; they get a point. You get pushed out; they get a point. You get thrown to your back; match is over."

The World of Warcraft development team began our journey into World of Warcraft: Forever with ambitions that grew and evolved over time. Our aim has always been to uphold the original WoW era aesthetic, while giving players more choice in how they experience Azeroth.
Over the course of development, we have been aligning on the right range of fidelity and what feels like it belongs in the WoW: Forever world and what does not. The team has learned much in the process, and that will continue to strengthen more with future content.
Along the way, there were some ideas the team wanted to explore that ultimately didn’t quite meet the consistency and cohesion we are aiming for. To align with our goals better, we are taking aim at updating some of those visuals for the future. Here is one example of how we are revisiting the High Definition (HD) Skyborne Druid forms.
We removed a bit of the softness, added more detailed fur textures, and adjusted the color saturation. The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world.
In choosing to offer an SD or HD toggle for player characters, we focused on the pre-existing races from original World of Warcraft since many people have an attachment to those models. However, we have heard feedback that the HD Skyborne can be jarring by contrast when placed in the same world as the SD models and world, and we agree.
So, for those of us that prefer the look of SD models and want more choice, Skyborne player characters (and yes SD Druid forms) are in development and arriving early 2027. We look forward to sharing more information closer to that date. For now, here is an early work in progress image.
This is just the start of our journey, and the whole team is thrilled with the reception for World of Warcraft: Forever . As we continue refining this vision together, we look forward to what lies ahead—for the Horde! For the Alliance! Forever!

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short.
The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use.
On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity.
However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail.
When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens , it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents".
Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive."
The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating.
OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work.
In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder.
The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases.
But Common Sense Media's new research determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable.
An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete."
"We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said.
While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide.
The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents.
It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert.
In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found.
The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour.
"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said.
The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common.
This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta , TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms.
OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT.
The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT.
OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident.

Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)
Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.
The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.
Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”
He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”
The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.
Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

articles.title_zh: Judo: Grigalashvili claims fourth world title as Kaju reigns again
articles.content_orig:
Baku is the stage for the middleweights on day 4 of the World Judo Championships.
At -63kg, reigning World Champion KAJU Haruka has never lost a contest on the World Judo Tour, and here in Baku she was determined to keep that record intact. She confidently earned her place in the final, aiming to keep her red backpatch for another year and continue her remarkable run.
She’d face Kerem PRIMO , who was entering not only her first World Championship final, but her first ever World Judo Tour final. It was the biggest moment of her career, and standing across from her would be one of the sport’s most formidable champions.
In the final, KAJU used her trademark groundwork to take control of the contest. Once in ne-waza, the Japanese judoka was clinical, extending her unbeaten run to 40 contests and taking her place at the top of the podium in Baku.
Football Legend Mr Lothar MATTHÄUS awarded the medals.
Triple World Champion, Georgian legend Tato GRIGALASHVILI was here to add a fourth World title to his collection in the -81kg category. After settling for silver last year, one of judo’s most dominant forces had another World gold firmly within his reach.
Facing him was Azerbaijan’s own Zelim TCKAEV who was looking to upgrade last year's World bronze medal to a history making World gold in his home nation. With the support of his home fans cheering on, could he rise to the challenge and become World Champion?
The atmosphere was electric as the final got underway, and GRIGALASHVILI rose to the occasion. The Georgian delivered when it mattered most, securing victory and with it a fourth World title, further cementing his place among judo’s modern greats.
Azerbaijan Judo Federation President Mr Rashad NABIYEV awarded the medals.
That’s it for day 4 in the land of fire.

articles.title_orig: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.title_zh: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.content_orig:
Pennsylvania’s explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it’s the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania’s health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April , when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths— a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, measles outbreaks and cases have come roaring back in the past few years. A large outbreak in Texas that spanned January­–August 2025 ended with 762 cases , while an outbreak in South Carolina ended in April with 997 cases , the previous record holder. Pennsylvania exceeds that handily with its 1,066 outbreak-linked cases as of today. With 34 new infections reported since Monday, the outbreak does not appear to be close to ending.
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Elimination is earned and maintained with vaccination rates that prevent continuous transmission of the virus during a 12-month period. In November, experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—which acts as a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data on whether the US has lost its measles elimination status. Experts widely expect the US has lost the status. Canada lost its elimination status in 2025.
The last measles outbreak that was larger than the current one in Pennsylvania was an outbreak in New York, which spanned 1990–1991 and infected more than 4,500 in all.
Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency over rising measles cases there. There have been at least 108 cases in the state. The emergency declaration expands the pool of healthcare workers who can provide measles vaccinations, newly including paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists, and midwives. It also allows nurses, in addition to physicians, to order measles tests.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement. “That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 3,887 measles cases nationwide for the year. That is the highest tally in the US since 1991, when there were 9,643 cases. Experts are becoming yet more anxious as measles outbreaks stretch into the fall; in the pre-vaccine era, measles was typically a virus of the late winter and early spring . Experts are concerned that spread could accelerate further in favorable conditions.

articles.title_orig: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.title_zh: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.content_orig:

Family members of victims of the Oct. 7 attack gather today at the Nova music festival site in Re'im, Israel. Â Erik Marmor / Getty
Tens of thousands of people gathered at Yarkon Park in Tel Aviv to attend a national memorial ceremony to commemorate the anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.
Organized by the families of October 7 , the ceremony was held for the third year to mourn victims of the attacks.
âOne thousand and ninety-six days of loss have passed,â said actress Shani Cohen, who co-hosted the ceremony alongside Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who lost his wife and two daughters in the attacks. âRemembering those who begged for help from within safe rooms engulfed in flames; those who hid in dumpsters, in bullet-riddled restroom stalls, and in shelters packed with people.â
Three years ago, militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israelâs yearslong military offensive in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people.
Hundreds of bereaved families, hostages and survivors of the attacks participated in the ceremony, sharing their stories of grief, alongside emotional musical performances from well-known Israeli artists.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog spoke at the memorial ceremony held at the site of the Nova Festival near Reâim in southern Israel, where hundreds of festivalgoers were murdered and abducted during the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks three years ago.
"We are here to tell their story and to remember and reflect and reminisce in this solemn day and say to the world, we shall dance again, we shall live again," he said. "This whole region, which was attacked barbarically on October 7, is now rebuilding, and it will double its population in the next few years, and people have chosen to come here and to live here and to say yes, we shall continue."
Herzog called on the international community to support efforts to disarm Hamas and combat Iran.
âWe are a nation like all nations. We have the inherent right to defend ourselves and fight terror. But we yearn for peace, and we want our neighbors to live in peace as well,â Herzog said.
President Donald Trumpâs Board of Peace paid tribute to Israelis and Palestinians in a statement today that said it was âstriving to create the conditions for a lasting peace through the demilitarization and deradicalization of Gaza.â
The body, which Trump has billed as part of the solution to a series of global conflicts, said in a statement that its effort was âdefined by pragmatic solutions, not statements or slogans.â
âGenuine and durable security for Israel is the foundation on which an peace must be built, and it is the surest guarantee that no October 7 will ever happen again,â it added.
At least one Palestinian was killed and 14 injured when Jewish settlers attacked olive farmers near the town of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported today.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said that its teams treated two people for gunshot wounds and three who had been beaten, the news agency reported.
According to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), some 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks in the West Bank since 2023.
Between Jan. 1 and July 24, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians, according to the latest data available from OCHA. Three Israelis were killed over the same period, the data shows.
Without a traditional distributor, a documentary that charts the Israeli militaryâs systematic killing of civilians, arrives in a limited number of U.S. theaters this month after sparking an intense backlash in Israel.
Israelis Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, both Academy Award-winning filmmakers, faced intense backlash at home following the documentary's premiere last month at the Venice Film Festival â where it earned an unprecedented 25-minute standing ovation.
Szor and Abraham pose with the Special Jury Prize Award at the Venice Film Festival. Â Rocco Spaziani / Mondadori Portfolio via Getty
The documentary, based on insider accounts from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, sparked outrage among Israeli officials , even spurring calls to consider criminal charges against the documentarians and strip them of their citizenship.
After showings at New Yorkâs IFC Center, the documentary will open Oct. 9 in cities including Austin, Chicago, Los Angeles and Seattle. It will also be available to stream for free on The Guardianâs website in late November.
âI felt that we have a responsibility, from our position, to also talk to the people who did it themselves and to bring this insider testimony, hoping that this will make the denial of what is happening harder,â Abraham told NBC News last month.
The Israel Defense Forces published a 10-page rebuttal last week, claiming the documentary is âbased on substantial factual errors stemming from a misrepresented and manipulative depiction of reality.â
Meanwhile, in an unusual step, Israel's Embassy in the U.S. was promoting a similarly titled documentary, "NAZA: The Real Story," which features senior IDF officials defending their conduct in Gaza.
The term genocide has increasingly been used by human rights bodies and independent experts to refer to Israel's actions in Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, despite emphatic Israeli and American denials.
Israel has said it abides by international law and the accusation distorts the legal definition of genocide. It also contends that the war in Gaza is an existential conflict with a foe that regularly uses civilians as human shields.
More than 74,000 people have been killed across the Gaza Strip since the war began, according to figures from the Palestinian Health Ministry.
In September 2025, an independent commission established by the U.N. Human Rights Council published a report concluding that Israel had committed genocide, citing widely accepted definitions under long-standing international conventions.
âIt is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the Genocide Convention,â said Navi Pillay, chair of the commission.
"Explicit statements by Israeli civilian and military authorities and the pattern of conduct of the Israeli security forces indicate that the genocidal acts were committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, Palestinians in the Gaza Strip as a group," the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a statement at the time.
In October 2025, the U.N.'s Special Rapporteur for human rights in the Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, alleged that the "ongoing genocide in Gaza is a collective crime, sustained by the complicity of influential third states that have enabled longstanding systemic violations of international law by Israel."
Leading Israeli human rights organization BâTselem also published a report in July 2025 concluding that Israel was committing genocide.
"Statements by senior Israeli officials and actions on the ground prove beyond any doubt that, in Israelâs eyes, the entire population of the Gaza Strip is the target," it said, adding to similar findings from groups including Amnesty International and Physicians for Human Rights Israel.
