articles.title_orig: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
articles.title_zh: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
articles.content_orig:
Researchers say a small fossil from the middle Jurassic provides some of the oldest evidence of chewing and swallowing as well as suckling — all distinctly mammalian traits. Chang-Fu Zhou/Shandong University of Science and Technology hide caption
Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.
"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo , a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.
It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.
This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature , was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.
Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.
"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.
The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.
"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."
One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.
The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.
An artistic rendering of Megacauda sungei . The animal was the size of a chihuahua and a bit of a mutt. Its back end resembled a platypus but its sharp teeth suggested it was a predator. April Neander/University of Chicago hide caption
These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.
"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.
There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.
The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.
The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.
With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.
This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.
The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."
Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.
Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.
"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."
This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.
"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor , a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."
Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.
"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."
For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.
"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."
By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

articles.title_orig: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.title_zh: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.content_orig:
Take a closer look at the "Make AI Work for Americans Act," and learn why it's important to help workers and families navigate AI disruption.
While there’s no consensus on exactly how artificial intelligence will affect workers, it’s clear that the technology will change who works and how they work. On September 24, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly introduced a bill called the Make AI Work for Americans Act . It prioritizes helping workers and families navigate the disruption that AI will cause through a federal trust fund paid for by the large AI companies set to profit most from AI’s boom.
In the past three years, the cumulative value of AI-linked firms has increased by $27 trillion across the value of the entire U.S. stock market; this accounts for 36% of value. There have been persistent concerns about whether this enormous spending—including on physical infrastructure and software development—is part of a bubble . Right now, this  technology is important to economic growth, as AI spending accounted for 40% of U.S. economic growth in the past year.
There are growing concerns about what the growth of AI means for American workers. OpenAI predicted that in the short term, 18% of jobs were at risk of automation, and 24% may see declining employment as the composition of tasks within occupations shifts.
Some estimates have found that of the highly AI-exposed workers, about 70% may be able to adapt fairly easily. But adaptation will likely be harder for over 6 million workers who are primarily employed in clerical and administrative roles.
What we can say now is that it’s likely that the effects of AI on workers will be concentrated in certain occupations. Last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released AI exposure categories organized by occupation that track how well the capabilities of AI match job tasks, and over 200 occupations are facing very high exposure , such as customer service representatives and web developers. The billion (trillion?) dollar question is whether occupations that are highly exposed will be able to adapt .
It’s also clear that people are worried about how AI is going to impact their jobs. A 2026 poll on AI found that 7 in 10 Americans think that AI will cut jobs. Polling from Groundwork Collaborative and Ipsos found that only 6% of respondents believe that the benefits of AI will mostly or all go to workers, and two-third of workers say that AI will make work harder, not easier.
Workers are doing their best to keep up, and a March 2026 national survey found that to compete with AI tools or avoid potential layoffs, 81% of workers are changing their behavior at work.
In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, universities are focused on developing technologies for physical AI , and the city is now home to 100 AI and robotics organizations. At the same time, Pittsburgh residents have pushed back against data centers due to their impact on the environment, pollution, and energy costs. Allegheny County is considering prohibiting data center development on county-owned land, and Pennsylvania has slowed data center development statewide.
In Iowa, rural communities like Salix are pushing back against data center projects; eight counties in the state already have moratoriums on data center development. Across the country, rural counties account for about two-thirds of planned data center projects, but they tend to see fewer benefits from these investments compared to cities. When a data center opens in a county, employment rises on average by about 3.5% and wages by 5%, but the gains from investment are experienced far more in urban counties than rural ones.
A third of South Carolinians believe that their employers will not protect them from having their jobs replaced by AI. At the same time, companies like Google are investing billions in the state’s cloud and AI infrastructure, i.e. data centers : Google’s 2025 investment is one of the largest technology investments in state history at $9 billion dollars .
Legislation like the Make AI Work for Americans Act is an important step and crucial part of supporting workers and their communities through this AI disruption. Importantly, it asks the companies profiting most from this technology to invest in the workers facing changing labor opportunities.
Heather Boushey is a professor of practice at the Kleinman Center. Boushey served in the Biden administration as a member of the Council of Economic Advisers and chief economist to the President’s Investing in America cabinet.

articles.title_orig: 'Indigenous People in the Modern World' theme reflects modern representation at Oct. 12 event
articles.title_zh: 'Indigenous People in the Modern World' theme reflects modern representation at Oct. 12 event
articles.content_orig:
Stuart James, a songwriter and producer from the Spirit Lake Reservation in North Dakota, will perform at "The Joyfull: Feast Edition" at 6 p.m. on Oct. 12 in Alumni Hall. Credit: Photo provided . All Rights Reserved .
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — The Center for the Performing Arts will celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day with "The Joyfull: Feast Edition" at 6 p.m. Oct. 12 in Alumni Hall, HUB-Robeson Center. The free collaborative event will feature food, entertainment and conversation about modern Indigenous representation.
Jacinta Garcia, community support and belonging specialist at the Paul Robeson Cultural Center, explained the importance of this year’s theme, “Indigenous People in the Modern World.”
“So often, we are typically represented in the past, the buckskin, the feathers, the more traditional pieces,” Garcia said. “It's really important to us to showcase what Native People are doing now.”
With the theme in mind, the Indigenous Peoples’ Student Association selected Stuart James as a musical artist for the event. James is a Dakota Sioux rapper, songwriter and producer from the Spirit Lake Reservation in North Dakota.
James uses his music as a form of storytelling about common experiences in the Indigenous community, taking inspiration from artists like J. Cole, Nas and Red Hot Chili Peppers. James said his song “Speak For” reflects his inspiration from J. Cole and dives into his perspective on social issues on the reservation.
“I really go into my perspective and how I view some of the social issues on the reservation,” James said. “It’s not so much to say I’m speaking and telling their story for them; this song is for those people who feel like they don’t have a voice or feel like they don’t know how to express themselves.”
Growing up, James said he would spend time at his grandmother’s house watching a DVD performance of the Indigenous comedy duo, James and Ernie Comedy, who will also be performing at the Joyfull event.
“Seeing them kind of inspired me to understand that I have that capability to be on the same type of stages,” James said. “It's just a full-circle moment for me to be there performing with them, as well, so I'm very excited for that.”
Garcia said he hopes that this event inspires attendees to not only follow the artists featured, but to explore and support up-and-coming Indigenous artists across “Turtle Island,” a traditional term some tribes use for the North American continent.
“Whether it's artists that are now in comedy, in hip hop, in all of these different avenues that our students want to get into, it's really important to see them represented there,” Garcia said. “It's super-important for the Penn State community to see us as we are today.”
Along with the artists, the "Feast" aspect of the event is also intentionally designed to represent current students. According to Garcia, because there is a large Navajo presence within the Penn State Indigenous student population, the menu will feature blue corn mush along with bison meatballs.
The meal will also have wild rice, a staple of the Ojibwe and Three Fires Nation; and strawberries, which are important to all nations, but specifically the creation stories of the nations across the North and Northeast.
Laenee McCoy, IPSA’s treasurer, said the opportunity to try new foods and recipes from different cultures leaves an impact on the broader Penn State community.
“I know that as an ally I hadn’t heard of or tried some of the dishes we have had in past years, so it was really cool to try them and learn more about the traditions behind them,” McCoy said. “IPSA has put a lot of work into creating opportunities for Indigenous culture to thrive and be seen, so I hope people take advantage of everything the events throughout the day have to offer.”
"The Joyfull: Feast Edition" will be hosted in partnership with the Indigenous Peoples Faculty/Staff and Student Alliances, Paul Robeson Cultural Center, Penn State Student Affairs and the Center for the Performing Arts.
“We could not do it without our partners,” Garcia said. “Our partnerships, our allies are absolutely key to ensuring that our very small group — because we are so underrepresented — that the message gets out, that we’re supported, that we’re projecting that message outward to the entire university, but also the State College community as well.”

articles.title_orig: French PM tries to defuse anger over schools, fuel and agriculture in sweeping speech
articles.title_zh: French PM tries to defuse anger over schools, fuel and agriculture in sweeping speech
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday pledged to address protesting high school students’ concerns while also announcing the release of strategic fuel reserves to lower prices.
"The anger among young people didn't come out of nowhere," Lecornu said as he addressed the nation.
The center-right prime minister said his government’s first policy responses to protesters’ concerns — including run-down schools, a shortage of substitute teachers, and a desire for more manageable schedules — would come later this month. The government will consider submissions on a public platform set up Tuesday to allow students to voice their grievances.
On Tuesday, between 256,000 people, according to police, and 450,000, according to organizers, joined demonstrations across France. Unions, teachers and left-wing political parties took to the streets in solidarity with high school students.
But discontent in France extends beyond schools. A surge in fuel prices, triggered by the U.S.-led war in Iran, has added to concerns about the cost of living.
Online calls for a Yellow Jackets -style protest on Oct. 17 have emerged in response to rising fuel prices.
"Last Friday, [the G7] decided to release strategic [fuel] reserves... As part of this effort, we will make 10 million barrels of diesel from our reserves available to distributors in France," Lecornu announced, claiming that the supply increase would lower diesel prices by €0.12 to €0.18 per liter.
France still has 8 million barrels of oil products to release under a wider deal brokered in March after the outbreak of the war in Iran, and had privately signaled Wednesday morning that it might release an additional 2 million barrels of diesel on top of that, as POLITICO reported earlier on Wednesday . It's unclear whether the 10 million figure includes that earlier commitment.
The French energy ministry did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Lecornu also reached out to French farmers, who have regularly protested in recent years to draw attention to the sector’s economic hardships. “Among those hardest hit by the accumulation of these crises are our farmers,” Lecornu said.
He said new measures to supplement an emergency bill for farmers, which already includes more than €1 billion in spending , would be unveiled Thursday.
Nicolas Camut contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Fed Minutes Show Officials Saw More Work to Do to Quell Inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed Minutes Show Officials Saw More Work to Do to Quell Inflation
articles.content_orig: Federal Reserve officials expect they will raise interest rates again before the end of the year to head off inflation that has run above target for more than five years, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. But the meeting summary provided no indication of when specifically policymakers expected to raise benchmark rates – only that persistently higher prices and a stable labor market likely would lead to a second hike this year. The Fed next decides on rates on Oct. 28 and then again on Dec. 9. "With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the document stated. That position came with a note of caution. "Participants emphasized, however, that they approached each meeting with an open mind and decisions at future meetings would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks," the minutes said. Coming off the meeting, which featured tough inflation talk from Chairman Kevin Warsh during his subsequent news conference, markets started betting the Fed would follow the Sept. 16 hike with another move at the late October meeting. However, recent inflation data and comments from leading Fed officials indicate that at least for October, another increase is unlikely. The Fed's preferred gauge – the personal consumption expenditures price index – showed core inflation at 3% for August and headline at 3.4%. While both readings were still well north of the central bank's 2% target, they were considerably lower than expectations, benefiting in part from changes in the way some of the inputs are calculated. Discussion at the September meeting showed officials see risks that inflation will prove sticky, while the labor market is "close to maximum employment" and economic growth overall has picked up. The vote to raise the benchmark funds rate by a quarter percentage point was unanimous, despite prior indications that several key officials were reluctant to hike. "Many participants emphasized that a higher path for the target range would be prudent on risk-management grounds, providing insurance against inflation remaining persistently above target due to stronger-than-expected demand or further adverse supply shocks," the summary said. As a group, the Federal Open Market Committee indicated one more hike this year, then none in 2027. Of the 18 FOMC officials who submitted forecasts, 16 said they expected another increase. Warsh has not submitted a forecast since taking the position in May. During his news conference, he described the rate rise as removing "a dose of accommodation" from monetary policy, a remark that Wall Street analysts pored over and took to mean that additional increases could be on the way. But several other officials since then have stressed that the Fed doesn't need to rush, while inflation data has been at least a bit more encouraging even if short-term expectations have risen considerably. Market-based indicators for inflation are still elevated, and a fresh survey released Wednesday by the New York Fed showed consumer fears over rising prices in the next year are at their highest since May 2023. Treasury yields have been soaring as well, hitting levels not seen since 2002. Officials at the meeting discussed the rise in yields, attributing them to expectations for higher rates from the Fed as well as the build-out in artificial intelligence and solid economic growth. Staff economists also noted that some of the surge may have come from "uncertainty related to the U.S. Treasury's announcement and implementation of the buyback program." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August announced his department would ramp up its buybacks of already-issued long-dated debt. However, the move has had little impact on yields, which are around their highest levels since 2002.

articles.title_zh: The Human Link: Computer Science for Today’s Complex World
articles.content_orig:
Whitman faculty and students are envisioning the future of computer science—and it’s about human connection
Painting with a sonic palette. Alice Chan ’27 traveled to Singapore with Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock to present EchoField at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference. Conference-goers were even able to add their own sounds and collaborate on a sonic map of the conference experience.
In a dark room, a vibrant colorscape spills over the floor. With each step you take, the sounds of Tokyo slowly emerge around you—a meandering patchwork of sonic memories corresponding to the swirl of colors at your feet: Ambient noise in a temple is bright white. Clattering wind is pale aqua. Pattering rain is red.
This is EchoField—an immersive, interactive audio archive developed by Alice Chan ’27 as a final project for her Computer Science course, Your Life in Sound (CS-100A), taken in her junior year. The class is taught by Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock , who encourages her students to think expansively about how humans interact with sound and how creating digital audio archives can connect people more closely with their experiences.
To create EchoField, Chan uploaded brief sound clips she recorded while studying abroad in Tokyo, pairing each with a color. As she started recording sounds in her life, she realized their power to evoke emotion and memory. “When you explore, you listen to the audio and reflect on what happened back then for yourself,” she says.
Chan, a Davis United World College Scholar from Hong Kong, who is studying Japanese while designing her own major in Human-Computer Interaction, hopes to become a user-experience designer, making technology easier for people to use.
EchoField came from her desire to create an app where users could immerse themselves in—and share—the sounds of daily life. She’d learned some coding skills in past classes, but used “vibe coding,” or collaborating with an AI program to write code, to create the first version of EchoField.
I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways. I believe in its potential to create even more connection.
Wirfs-Brock was impressed with Chan’s concept and enthusiasm and invited her to work together to refine EchoField and submit a paper about it to conferences. They teamed up with William Bares , Associate Professor of Computer Science, who specializes in designing interactive experiences using motion tracking.
The group helped EchoField leap off the computer screen and into the physical world. Using motion-capture technology, people can now explore a projected image of the colorful archive as audio fills the air, “being in the sound instead of just listening to it,” Chan says.
In June 2026, Chan and Wirfs-Brock presented EchoField to technology researchers from around the world at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference in Singapore.
Chan says Whitman has given her the opportunity to study many aspects of how humans interact with technology, including courses in Computer Science, Psychology , Human-Centered Design and Sociology . She believes that technology is important for bringing people together in a global society, where we’re often far apart.
“I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways,” she says. “I believe in its potential to create even more connection.”
Play with a sonic palette of sounds recorded in Walla Walla and Singapore. Try it now. Click on the library icon to start exploring sounds recorded around campus, at the Designing Interactive Systems conference and beyond.
‘They want to change the world.’ Today’s Whitman students are searching for innovative ways to harness computer science in the service of humanity, says Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science William Bares. And the department is evolving to give them the skills to do it.
The values embodied in Chan’s project—human innovation, creativity and empathy—will always be an essential part of computer science, Bares says.
As Chair of Whitman’s Computer Science Department, Bares envisions an inter­disciplinary future where computer scientists and experts in other fields come together, sometimes in collaboration with artificial intelligence, to discover the ideas that AI can’t come up with on its own.
“Creative ideas, entrepreneurial ideas, often come from thinking about a problem from a different perspective, being familiar with different fields,” he says.
Bares and his colleagues in the Computer Science Department are working to design a flexible curriculum that allows students to incorporate ideas from different disciplines and be more adaptable in the face of rapid changes in the computing world.
By leaning into its liberal arts mission, Whitman can help Computer Science students broaden and deepen their skills in ethics, philosophy, communication, critical thinking and human-centered design, Bares says.
Those fundamentally human skills give graduates an edge in a tech industry where traditional career paths are increasingly being reshaped by generative AI.
By providing more opportunities to create projects like EchoField, Whitman can help students build a portfolio that showcases their ability to create impactful work about meaning­ful topics.
“Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future,” Bares says. “These are skills that build multiple pathways for students, so they’ve got that ability to be flexible, which is what the current market demands.”
Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future.
—William Bares, Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science
Bares compares traditional computer science courses to a single-crop field: focused on one subject, such as data structures, without much cross-pollination.
His vision for Whitman’s Computer Science program is to make space for classes that he compares to meadows: intricate and diverse, drawing in other disciplines the way an abundant landscape attracts and energizes wildlife.
Introductory-level classes like Your Life in Sound innovate by giving students an early opportunity to be creative and imagine pathways to research and entrepreneurship beyond the traditional software developer role, Bares says.
In summer 2024, the faculty met to rewrite the department’s learning outcomes and begin reshaping course offerings and requirements. The updated curriculum emphasizes communication, collaboration and self-directed learning, as well as critical evaluation of computational technologies—considering whether technologies are efficient and ethical and thinking about the impact they have on society, communities and environments.
Bares says this work is inspired by students’ passionate interest in making the world better. “They want to do positive things for the environment, they want to help people, they want to know that what they’re learning and doing has a benefit.”
Some of the new courses and requirements have already been rolled out, and much like product testing, the department is gathering student feedback so that faculty can continue to improve their course offerings and teaching.
Bares hopes that the next iteration of the Computer Science curriculum will make room for even more courses like Your Life in Sound and innovative senior capstone projects, such as interactive data installations, independent research and startup launches.
In concert with interdisciplinary classes, Bares also dreams of creating more opportunities for students to showcase their projects to the campus community and the public—and he envisions larger, more accessible spaces for these immersive experiences on campus.
“This is the future of computer science,” Bares says. “We believe this is going to be what will excite students to want to come here, and also faculty to want to come here and be part of this.”

articles.title_orig: A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.title_zh: A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.content_orig:
By OLIVIA ALLHUSEN, FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 20:40 EDT, 7 October 2026 | Updated: 21:33 EDT, 7 October 2026
A giant tortoise approaching his 195th birthday may hold the secret to a longer life after scientists discovered parts of his body appear far younger than his remarkable age.
Jonathan, the world's oldest known living land animal, was born before Queen Victoria came to the throne and has long spent his days on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena.
Now researchers have discovered signs that some of the biological machinery inside his cells appears remarkably youthful, despite his estimated age of 194.
The findings could help scientists investigate how some animals resist the effects of ageing, although further research is needed to establish what they might mean for humans.
And the beloved tortoise is still going strong after scammers falsely announced his death earlier this year in an apparent bid to solicit cryptocurrency donations.
Scientists sequenced Jonathan's genome, his complete set of genetic instructions, using DNA collected from a cheek swab by his vet, Dr Joe Hollins.
The results, published in the journal Science Advances, revealed genetic variants associated with repairing damaged DNA, regulating metabolism and protecting against cancer.
But one of the most intriguing discoveries concerned his mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply cells with energy.
Jonathan, the world's oldest known living land animal, was born before Queen Victoria came to the throne and has long spent his days on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena
Vet Joe Hollins, pictured left with Jonathan
Prince Edward met the 194-year-old in 2024
Declining mitochondrial function has been linked to ageing and age-related diseases.
Researchers examined chemical tags on Jonathan's DNA that help regulate how his genes behave, comparing them with those of other giant tortoises.
While many of these patterns resembled those found in older animals, the patterns associated with mitochondrial function looked more like those of much younger tortoises.
Stephen Clark, a researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation, told the Guardian: 'His mitochondria must be especially stable and that's an insight into longevity in general. It's important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.'
Scientists have yet to establish whether these patterns help explain Jonathan's extraordinary lifespan, or how large a role they might play.
The team also identified differences involving DNA repair and the maintenance of telomeres, the protective caps on chromosomes.
DNA damage accumulates as organisms age, while telomeres become shorter, a process thought to contribute to ageing.
Jonathan also shares some genes with other long-lived species, including naked mole rats, which can live to 40 and rarely develop cancer.
Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies ageing at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an author of the study, told the New York Times: 'We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive.'
Obtaining Jonathan's DNA proved a delicate operation.
Dr Hollins had to hold his head with a thick welding glove and carefully prop open his sharp beak to swab the inside of his cheek.
An initial attempt produced a sample covered in half-chewed carrot, one of the tortoise's favourite snacks.
Researchers were not allowed to take blood because of the risk of infection, and the saliva sample had to leave the island by boat.
Jonathan lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of St Helena's governor, around 1,200 miles off Africa's west coast.
His exact birth date is unknown, but he was already fully grown when he arrived on the island in 1882, suggesting he was at least 50.
The tortoise welcomed the future Queen Elizabeth II, as well as George VI and the Queen Mother, to the British overseas territory of St Helena in 1947, pictured
He was brought to St Helena from the Seychelles in the 1880s and lived on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's Governor
Should scientists try to unlock animal secrets to extend human lifespans, or let nature take its course?
That puts his estimated birth year at 1832, before Queen Victoria took the throne and before Charles Darwin visited the Galapagos Islands.
In April, a fake account on X posing as Dr Hollins claimed Jonathan had died.
The post spread widely, but the real vet exposed the deception and said the account was asking for cryptocurrency donations.
St Helena's governor, Nigel Phillips, also checked on Jonathan after being contacted by the Guardian and found him asleep beneath a tree.
Despite cataracts and the loss of his sense of smell, Jonathan continues to enjoy life, retaining excellent hearing and a strong libido.
When Dr Hollins took over his care in 2009, the tortoise was struggling to forage and had a soft, crumbling beak.
Regular hand-feeding helped him regain weight and develop a hard beak within six months to a year.
Scientists caution that his protected surroundings, fresh vegetables and veterinary care could also help explain his exceptional age.
But his biology offers promising avenues for further investigation.
Steve Austad, a biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, told the New York Times: 'Each of these long-lived species has some kind of special trick. And some of those may turn out to be relevant to human aging.'

articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

articles.title_orig: Two-Thirds of the World’s First Computer Is Still Missing Beneath the Sea
articles.title_zh: Two-Thirds of the World’s First Computer Is Still Missing Beneath the Sea
articles.content_orig:
Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:
It was in the spring of 1900 that a group of waylaid sponge divers first stumbled upon a lost Greek ship after taking refuge on the island of Antikythera during a storm. When the storm subsided, the divers, who shared one brass diving helmet strapped to the ship with ropes, began plying the waters along the island’s eastern edge. One diver, Elias Stadiatis, pulled sharply on his rope. When he reached the surface, Stadiatis frantically described a scene of carnage—rotting corpses of women and horses strewn across the seafloor. The ship’s captain, Dimitrios Kontos, dove down to see for himself.
One of the divers—most reports say Kontos—later resurfaced with a bronze arm, part of a lost masterwork of antiquity . By complete chance, these divers had discovered the world’s richest shipwreck and inadvertently became history’s first underwater archaeologists .
When the divers, now employed by the Greek government, returned months later, excavating the site proved difficult. This part of the Aegean was frequently besieged by tumultuous waves. Furious storms were common, and the shipwreck had settled at a 45-degree angle, perilously close to the same rocky cliffs that likely ended its voyage two millennia prior. Some 300 years after the wreck, a rockslide had further entombed the vessel.
But even in these challenging conditions, the divers exhumed dozens of containers called amphorae—what Foley describes as the 55-gallon drums of the ancient world—along with perfume jars, glass bowls, jewels, coins, and many of those “corpses,” which turned out to be not-so-spooky bronze and marble statues. The divers could only stay submerged for about 10 minutes, Foley explains, and likely spent only a few minutes on the seafloor. The divers worked with rudimentary kit by today’s standards yet still somehow rigged up sculptures so they could be pulled from the water depths. “What they did was almost superhuman,” he says.
Foley’s own memories of diving at the island of Antikythera—he visited the site and its surrounding waters once or twice every year between 2011 and 2017 and estimates that he’s spent around 87 hours beneath the waves—contain two juxtaposing truths about the Aegean: It’s one of the most beautiful marine environments in the world and it’s very challenging to study.
During an expedition in September 2014, Foley and his colleagues—experts from the Hellenic Ministry of Culture and Sports’s Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities (EUA) and the Australian Centre for Field Robotics—planned to spend a week mapping the wreck with autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). They also had a crew of divers, armed with rebreathers and metal detectors, ready to scan the seafloor for ancient artifacts. Then they would debut a piece of heavy-duty diving equipment called the exosuit—picture a cross between Tony Stark’s Iron Man suit and the Michelin Man—into which divers could climb and explore depths too deep for scuba.
Foley and his team managed to get only four days of diving in and used the bulbous exosuit twice before the sky grew dark and strong winds rolled in.
Though rough weather scuttled their plans, they were still able to generate a three-millimeter-resolution map of the shipwreck and managed to recover an impressive collection of artifacts. On subsequent dive trips, he and his team uncovered more sculptures, a mysterious 100-kilogram lead weapon known as “the dolphin,” a nearly complete human skeleton, and a peculiar mechanism thought to be an ancient astronomical calendar and one of the earliest progenitors of the modern computer. Today, we call it the Antikythera mechanism.
Foley recalls peering over the cliff face on a particularly stormy day during that 2014 expedition, watching with awe as waves pummeled the shore near the site of the wreck: “It gave me a really good indication of what the conditions may have been like the night or day when this ship sank.”
Over the decades, experts have tried to piece together what exactly happened to this ship all those centuries ago. While some details shift among varying narratives of the ship’s fateful journey, the end result remains the same: At some point in the middle of the first century B.C.E., the Antikythera mechanism, thought to be the world’s first computer, came to rest in the salty sediments of the Aegean. Since then, mathematicians, clockmakers, metallurgists, astrophysicists, and underwater archaeologists have tried to make sense of this fragmented, corroded, and maddening amalgamation of gears, pins, and dials.
For two millennia, the mechanism lay untouched in its watery tomb more than 100 feet below the waves as time slowly trickled by, giving way to the birth of empires, the collapse into the Dark Ages, the rise of theocratic kingdoms, the foundation of nation-states, and the arrival of modern science.
It’s a wonder the mechanism survived at all, given the conditions it faced in the ocean. “If you go into many of the archaeological museums in Europe, all of the fabulous bronze sculptures primarily come from shipwrecks or from sites underwater,” Foley explains. At the time of antiquity, bronze was valuable. And because it was malleable, it could be easily repurposed. “You might make a statue of a Greek god, but once that religion goes out of fashion…you can melt [the statue] down and make church bells or artillery gun barrels,” he says.
But 2,000 years underwater didn’t do the Antikythera mechanism many favors. Seawater rich with salts and other chemical compounds reacted with the high amount of copper in the bronze mechanism, slowly corroding it and replacing it with a green-hued rock known as atacamite. Over time, silt and sand accumulated between the gear wheels, which eventually solidified into hunks of lumpy rock. Bits of wood found among the fragments suggest the mechanism was housed in an ornate wooden frame.
The device is almost as famous for its incompleteness as it is for its complexity. Now housed at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, Greece, only one-third of the roughly shoebox-sized mechanism, spread across 82 fragments of varying sizes, has been found. The rest has been lost to the sea.
More than a century later, the discoveries—and controversies—surrounding one of the most incredible archaeological finds in human history are only growing.

articles.title_orig: Expert tips for parents to prepare as flu season begins - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Expert tips for parents to prepare as flu season begins - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Flu season is beginning, and it's a time that can be stressful for busy parents and families.
Influenza, more commonly known as the flu, can be more serious than the common cold and other illnesses, especially for kids with chronic conditions and those under 5 years old, the Centers for Disease and Prevention notes.
To help parents prepare, ABC News spoke with Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, the chief executive officer of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, to get expert tips for parents to get ahead of the flu season.
The IDSA, as well as other physician groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommends everyone, including parents and kids over the age of 6 months, get a flu vaccine.
"The vast majority of really bad outcomes, the worst being death, but also including hospitalization for flu-related illness, occur in kids who are unvaccinated," Marrazzo said. "When you look at the worst flu years, for example, 2025, 2024, they were not good for kids. We had between 150 and 180 deaths in kids, and over 90% of the kids who died, unfortunately, were unvaccinated."
Young children between 6 months to 23 months old can receive an injection of the inactivated flu vaccine, while children between 2 to 8 years old have an option between the inactivated injection or an intranasal live attenuated flu vaccine -- a nasal spray.
"You can choose, in that young age period, between those two vaccines. That's nice because it helps avoid a shot in kids who are at that age, very concerned and very sensitive [to injections]," Marrazzo said, adding that the exception is that children with a compromised immune system or conditions such as asthma should not receive the nasal spray flu vaccine.
For children 9 years and older, they can receive an inactivated flu vaccine shot, an intranasal vaccine, or a recombinant flu vaccine.
Parents should encourage and remind children to practice good hygiene, including washing hands regularly and covering coughs, to keep sickness at bay.
But when respiratory symptoms do develop, influenza may appear similar to other respiratory viruses so having common medications on hand can help support the recovery process.
Flu symptoms may include fever, chills, a cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headaches, fatigue or gastrointestinal issues, such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC .
"It's good to have on hand things like child acetaminophen or Tylenol, or even ibuprofen like Advil or Motrin, because you can treat those fevers directly," Marrazzo said. "Otherwise, it's really supportive care. You want to make sure the kid is really well hydrated. Ideally, you'd like to have the child not be around other people in the household if you think it's the flu."
Parents should always consult with and talk to their child's pediatrician or doctor about any concerns about their child's health, including before and when they get sick or if they develop any new symptoms.
"If you have a very young child, certainly less than a year old, you don't want to mess around because you want to make sure they're OK," Marrazzo said. "[Other times to talk to your child's doctor are] if your child has serious medical conditions, asthma, cancer, or lung disease, if the baby or child is on dialysis. Those are some things that you want to pay special attention to."

articles.title_orig: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.title_zh: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.content_orig:
Whether you’re charging into battlegrounds with your faction or setting your sights on long-term PvP (Player vs. Player) goals, World of Warcraft: Forever brings a refreshed sense of purpose to every match-up. This approach gives players more reasons to take part throughout the season while preserving the spirit of competition that defined PvP in the original World of Warcraft .
When reimagining the PvP system, we wanted to keep the design pillar of “Approachable and Familiar” firmly in view: simplifying the original Honor System while staying true to its roots.
In World of Warcraft: Forever, PvP progression has two parts: Honor and Rank Points.
Honor is a currency players earn through taking part in PvP content. This includes defeating other players, completing battlegrounds, and finishing relevant PvP quests. Players also earn increased Honor in highlighted battlegrounds during their holiday weeks.
As part of these updates, we reviewed Honor gains across battlegrounds so acquisition rates are more consistent across the board. We want players to enjoy the full range of battleground maps without feeling compelled to choose Alterac Valley solely for Honor efficiency.
Rank Points come from PvP activities such as battlegrounds and relevant PvP quests, with holiday-week battlegrounds offering an additional boost. As players earn Rank Points, they advance through familiar PvP ranks from original World of Warcraft, working toward the ultimate titles of High Warlord for the Horde or Grand Marshal for the Alliance. Ranks have a weekly cap, retaining the foundation of the original system while making the journey more accessible.
Honor can be used to purchase two sets of PvP gear: one blue-quality set and one epic-quality set. The epic set requires the blue piece plus an Emboldened Seal to upgrade it, and Emboldened Seals have rank requirements players must reach before purchasing. There are also new and reworked items to fill gaps for specializations that were previously missing options. For example, Shaman now have healer, melee, and caster PvP gear sets they can acquire.
Below are the rank requirements for PvP item rewards:
Rank 1 - Tabard Rank 2 - PvP Trinket Rank 3 - Cloaks Rank 4 - Necklace Rank 5 - Combat Potions Rank 6 - Tabard Rank 7 - Battle Standard Rank 8 - Epic Bracers/Epic Belt Upgrade Token Rank 9 - Epic Boots Upgrade Token Rank 10 - Epic Gloves Upgrade Token Rank 11 - Mounts Rank 12 - Epic Legs/Epic Shoulders Upgrade Token Rank 13 - Epic Chest/Epic Helm Upgrade Token Rank 14 - Epic Weapons
To view your progress, you can open your Character Pane (Hotkey-C) then select the Player vs. Player tab on the right side of the interface. It will show you your rank, your current Rank Points, and what rewards are available for purchase based on your rank.
During a PvP season, players can progress through the ranks and earn Honor. Each season also includes a journey with weekly tasks to complete. Successfully completing those tasks grants Honor and Rank Points, and three tasks each season also grant a Legacy Point. Completing these tasks is part of the seasonal journey, and because they are tied to the Legacy System, they remain available to complete in future seasons.
With more ways to make progress each week and meaningful goals to pursue throughout the season, PvP in World of Warcraft: Forever gives players a clear path to jump in, compete, and keep building toward what comes next.

articles.title_orig: Travis Barker shares cryptic photo from hospital with Kourtney Kardashian by his side
articles.title_zh: Travis Barker shares cryptic photo from hospital with Kourtney Kardashian by his side
articles.content_orig:
Travis Barker is giving hints as to his current health status in a new post.
The Blink-182 drummer shared several photos from a hospital bed on Tuesday, with his wife, Kourtney Kardashian Barker, and daughter, Alabama Barker, by his side.
“My baby girl came with me,” he wrote over a picture on Instagram stories of him and Alabama. In the next slide, he shared a picture of him and Kourtney kissing, with the caption, “And my beautiful wife by my side.”
Barker himself was in a hospital gown with a surgical cap on, as well as an IV clearly in his arm and a blood pressure cuff around his bicep.
The reason for the hospital visit was not specified, but the next slide on Barker’s Instagram stories showed he was apparently back at home, filming his and Kourtney’s son Rocky riding a toy dinosaur.
Barker’s post comes three years after he underwent surgery on his finger for a torn ligament.
“It was a hard decision to make but ultimately I couldn’t continue to play the drums without it. It was inevitable that my finger would have dislocated again without fixing the torn ligament surgically,” he wrote on Instagram at the time. “So grateful for Dr. Shin and that my surgery was a success so that I can keep doing what I love and see you guys on tour soon.”
He also thanked fans, writing, “Thank you for all the love and prayers and understanding this week as I went into surgery.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Delays Threaten Funding for HIV Research
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Delays Threaten Funding for HIV Research
articles.content_orig:
Advocacy has always been the heartbeat of progress in the fight against HIV/AIDS. Now, more than ever, it is especially needed to ensure that innovation translates into real choices, equitable access and meaningful impact. In this issue, we highlight the power of coalition advocacy – from advocates working in partnership to shape research agendas and oppose policies that threaten progress, to ensuring communities have a voice in AI development and use, to the lessons learned from sustained, coalition-based advocacy that will shape what comes next.
Following advocacy by AVAC, advocates, researchers, scientific institutions and members of the US Congress , the White House dropped plans for an Executive Order that would have given an external review committee decision-making power over billions of dollars in biomedical research funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) .
The reversal came as the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Council and AIDS Research Advisory Committee met to discuss the proposed reorganization of NIAID that would eliminate the Division of Clinical Research and redistribute clinical research functions across the Institute – a move that threatens the incredible progress that has been achieved toward HIV treatment and prevention as well as potentially putting lives at risk. AVAC delivered a public comment at the meeting, urging NIH to withdraw the proposal, provide greater transparency and meaningful opportunities for community input, and immediately release delayed funding opportunities for the HIV Clinical Trials Networks and Centers for AIDS Research (CFARs).
Now, the picture has become even more complicated, with the NIH notifying HIV researchers last Friday that they should pause launching any new studies that had not yet enrolled participants and that would go beyond November 30 of next year when current funding expires.
The Save HIV Funding Campaign , which AVAC co-founded with PrEP4All and the HIV Medicine Association (HIVMA), requests organizations to consider signing on to this letter that urges Members of Congress to demand that the US Department of Health and Human Services approve the release of overdue Notices of Funding Opportunities (NOFOs) that fund the NIH HIV clinical trials networks and the CFARs for the next seven years. This funding is essential to the continuation of HIV research, including clinical trials that involve people who receive vital services. The deadline for signing on is Thursday, October 15th. For individuals in the US, please consider sending emails to your members of Congress through this link .
Read AVAC’s remarks on the proposed NIAID reorganization
At AIDS 2026 , advocates didn’t just join the conversation – they drove it. From HIV prevention choice and equitable access to community-led research and the future of HIV prevention , advocates brought bold priorities, lived experience and accountability to the center of the global HIV response. Across panels, protests, satellites and strategic meetings, communities made clear: there is no effective HIV response without community leadership. As WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus put it, communities are “its architects.” In AVAC’s latest blog , Senior Program Manager Navita Jain reflects on the power of communities at the conference, and AVAC’s top ten list compiles the takeaways influencing the field well beyond the conference.
Read how advocates led the narrative at AIDS 2026
AVAC’s Clinical Trial Design Academy (CTDA) brings together advocates with diverse perspectives and technical expertise to strengthen their ability to shape HIV prevention research. Through the network, members share knowledge, engage directly with researchers and work collectively to ensure community priorities inform research agendas and trial decisions . From shaping the People’s Research Agenda to influencing the design of the EXPrESSIVE trials of monthly oral alimatravir for PrEP , CTDA members are demonstrating the power of a connected, technically informed advocacy network to move research forward. As Kenyan CTDA member Simon Ondiek shared, “beyond the technical skills, the biggest impact has been the network we’ve built—a community that continues to learn from one another and ensure research remains responsive to community realities”. The CTDA meets in person this week—stay tuned for updates and outcomes.
Read about the CTDA’s collective impact on HIV prevention research
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is already being used in HIV programming, making the need for community leadership an urgent matter. “Community governance must be part of that infrastructure, not an advisory layer added at the end, but a legitimate source of expertise and authority in setting the rules,” writes ITPC Executive Director, Community Working Group Co-Lead of the Lancet Commission on AI + HIV, and AVAC Board Member Solange Baptiste . AVAC’s quarterly AI and HIV newsletter provides advocates with the information and resources to advance community prioritization in AI. The latest issue looks across important perspectives like Baptiste’s, alongside data from AIDS 2026 emerging tools, policy developments and research shaping how AI is developed, governed and used across HIV and global health.
Read the AI & HIV Newsletter
The CASPR Impact Report: Celebrating Growth, Inspiring the Future captures what is possible when long-term investment in African leadership, partnerships and coalition-based advocacy is matched with shared purpose. The Coalition to Accelerate and Support Prevention Research (CASPR) is an Africa-led movement that connects communities, researchers, policymakers, journalists and funders to transform HIV prevention advocacy . Over the past decade, CASPR proved that community-led coalitions are central to turning innovation into action and ensuring that advances in HIV prevention are shaped by the people they are meant to serve, while offering a blueprint for the future HIV prevention advocacy.
Read the CASPR Impact Report
Access Brid ge is an independent, Africa-anchored organization advancing timely, sustainable, and equitable introduction of and access to HIV prevention and related health products. To receive updates on Access Bridge’s work and impact, sign up for the newly launched newsletter.
STIWatch is AVAC’s resource for the sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) community to better understand and advocate for STI vaccine and diagnostics research, development and rollout. To receive the latest on data and new resources, sign up to receive updates on STI prevention.

articles.title_orig: Greens investigate party member behind Zionism motion
articles.title_zh: Greens investigate party member behind Zionism motion
articles.content_orig:
The Green Party has launched an investigation into party member Lubna Speitan, after it emerged she was listed in court documents as a "close friend" of a man later jailed for supporting al-Qaeda.
Speitan was behind a controversial Green Party conference motion which described Zionism as a form of racism.
A Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate and an investigation is underway."
In a post on Instagram, before the Green Party had confirmed its investigation to the BBC, Speitan said: "I reject all defamatory and nonsense claims made about me."
She added: "I reject all attempts to decontextualise past statements I have made."
"This is a classic distraction. I am not the conversation," she said, adding: "Racism is. Zionism is. The ethnic cleansing and genocide of Palestinians is. Let's talk about that."
In June, a UN commission of inquiry said Israel had deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Gaza Strip.
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence.
Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green Party conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".
The motion - which was approved by party members by 1,022 votes to 813 - also called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
The motion attracted criticism from opposition parties and some Jewish groups, who labelled it an "attack on the Jewish community".
Four out of five Green Party MPs also opposed the motion.
Adrian Ramsay, a former party leader and Green MP for Waveney Valley, said the motion was an "unhelpful distraction" and "wrong in principle" as "the Green Party has always supported the right to self-determination and that has to apply to all peoples".
Asked if he would consider leaving the party, Ramsay told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live he was "not ruling anything in or out at this stage".
"What I'm doing at this stage, and we're only a few days after the motion, is to talk carefully with colleagues to reflect both with Jewish Greens but also with Green MPs and other people in leading roles in the party to look at how best can we get things back on track," he said.
On Tuesday, the Jewish Chronicle reported the existence of a 2015 letter from Speitan in which she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham.
US prosecutors said Pham had been directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him.
He was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.
In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" who could provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state".
In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem".
She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that I and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed".
She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known."
There is no suggestion in the documents Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other.
Following the emergence of the letter on Tuesday afternoon, a Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate."
On Wednesday, the party released an updated statement adding "an investigation is under way".
The spokesperson said: "Lubna Speitan holds no party positions other than being a member."

articles.title_orig: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
articles.title_zh: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
articles.content_orig:
Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.
Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.
In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.
The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.
The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.
Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.
"It's like a penguin Mordor."
Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.
Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).
Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.
There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.
Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.
Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.
Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.
"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
The research is published in the journal Current Biology .

articles.title_orig: AMD’s Mark Papermaster: Exclusive Video Interview at World Summit AI
articles.title_zh: AMD’s Mark Papermaster: Exclusive Video Interview at World Summit AI
articles.content_orig:
Frances Haugen and Mikey Madison during an interview with TIME.
The Social Network helped define a generation of tech founders when it premiered in 2010: Written by Aaron Sorkin , it tells the story of Facebook’s founding by an ambitious, jilted college kid who imposes his will on the world. Now, in The Social Reckoning , Sorkin focuses on the ills of the company Facebook eventually became. He tells the story through the lens of Frances Haugen , a former employee who demonstrated through a trove of internal documents, leaked to the Wall Street Journal , that Facebook’s algorithm was stoking political division, that Instagram was contributing to body-image issues for teen girls, and that the company’s platforms were being used by drug dealers and human traffickers. CEO Mark Zuckerberg has denied his company, rebranded as Meta after Haugen’s leak, prioritized profit over safety. Mikey Madison, fresh off her Oscar for Anora , plays Haugen in the film. Madison and Haugen sat with TIME for their first interview together.
Madison: When I got the script, I knew about the Facebook Files, but I didn’t know Frances’ name. So I looked her up, and I was like, “She’s blonde and has blue eyes. Why does Aaron want me for this?” And he said, “I want you to try and build the character from my script.” But of course I read her memoir and tried to do my due diligence because there was so much I didn’t understand. I don’t have a personal relationship with social media at all.
Madison: It’s just something that never quite stuck. It’s something I never felt I could understand. When I was 13, I had an Instagram, but it kind of lived and died at that time and not for any particular reason or self-preservation.
Haugen: I first met Aaron a few months after I came forward as a whistleblower, and he wanted to figure out if it was possible to do a companion piece to The Social Network . After my memoir came out, he came back to me with this heavily underlined, sticky-noted, dog-eared copy.
Madison: I don’t know if much can prepare you for that. I’m not someone who naturally speaks in that rhythmic way. I don’t know anyone who does, except for maybe Aaron. It’s singular to his sensibilities as a screenwriter. I keep joking that Aaron has this internal stopwatch in his head. Every period, every comma is incredibly intentional, and the space between is timed, and we’re on a deadline. The first day on set, after seven or eight takes, he came in and was like, ‘OK, we’re starting to cook with a bit of gas here.’
Madison: But I also think it created a certain intensity.
Haugen: There’s a fidelity to it. [ Wall Street Journal reporter] Jeff [Horwitz] and I are both chatty people who talk quickly, so you do capture the excitement of when we were in the weeds.
Jeremy Allen White as Jeff Horwitz and Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen Courtesy of Sony
Haugen: We’re only in the first chapter of the settlements. We still have two major sets of settlements to go just in the United States. The school districts are bringing very large suits, which I’m expecting to have dollar values north of $100 billion, maybe $200 billion. And then we have the individual kids and family lawsuits. So far, we’ve only had one resolve, but it was $6 million to a single person . When you apply that across kids in the United States, you only need a fraction of 1% [of that amount], and it adds up to a trillion dollars.
Haugen: Mark is in a unique psychological circumstance in that there are very few founders in Silicon Valley who have the level of control he has at the scale he has...I think he’s just been isolated for so long it’s distorted his priorities.
Madison: I had less than half a day to work with him. We had one scene, but I was almost a background actor. I hope to be able to work with him in the future. His process is intriguing to me as an actress. The result is obviously very special.
Frances Haugen and Mikey Madison attend 'The Social Reckoning' world premiere on Oct. 04, 2026 in New York City Dimitrios Kambouris—Getty Images
Haugen: I think you can square the circle on capitalism and what is good for us. Five years ago, people in the United States used Instagram and Facebook more than they do today. And part of that is because Meta over-optimized for the short term instead of the long term. When you see unpleasant content, when you see AI slop and bullying and more ads, you’re less likely to use the product. Governance helps businesses make choices that optimize for the long term, which actually makes them more profitable long-term. So capitalism doesn’t have to be in conflict with safety. When it comes to AI, part of what makes it hard is the rate of change. I’m hopeful we’re going to have one or two more scary incidents, and then we’re going to be like, “Maybe we should do something sensible.”
Haugen: I went from someone who could ride 125 miles a day on a bike to being in a wheelchair in two and a half years. One day my leg turned blue and it turned out that I had a foot-long clot the girth of a cigar in my leg, and they had to do surgery multiple times. Unfortunately while I was in the hospital I had an allergic reaction to the blood thinner. During that time, I went through my worst fears. I lost my job because they thought I was faking being sick. My husband left me. I lost my health. And I came back from it. So I do feel that phase of my life changed my ability to take risks. In terms of the movie, Aaron Sorkin did a miraculous thing: He made typing at a computer compelling for two hours. But you have to make choices. Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.

The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
